text: Camera pixels (depth distribution plus offset) and radar points (Point Transformer V3) become 3D Gaussians, splatted into a 200 x 200 BEV, fused in four stages and decoded to seven map layers. This is our frozen foundation (K61, from E27: F1@1 0.867 against 0.624 for CRN); every head reads its cached features. Caveats: features are cleaner on its own scenes (0.93) than on unseen ones (0.82), no failure evaluation exists, FP32 only, vendored rasteriser is non-commercial. Use: keep as is; optionally export alpha coverage and per-modality maps.
extract: skip: our own foundation, already integrated

text: Penalises the squared distance of the fine-tuned weights from the pre-trained ones, an anchor instead of zero (register line only, no note). For us it was one factor of the E73 fine-tuning study of the route-conditioned head (K72); the sources give no L2-SP-specific gain, and the best head came from joint map-trust training plus weight averaging. It touches head fine-tuning only, not the frozen foundation or the graph chain. Context: already tried, no next step.

Per-pixel categorical depth distribution times a context vector lifts image features into a frustum, pooled into a 200 x 200 BEV at 0.5 m. It is the view-lifting technique in our register (K65) and holds the only frozen-versus-end-to-end row: a frozen ImageNet encoder loses about 11 IoU on drivable area (61.62 against 72.94), but that encoder is generic, not map-pretrained like ours. Camera-only and single-frame, so no head-side idea to take. Context: no action.

Interpolates linearly between the weights before and after fine-tuning with one coefficient, at no extra cost (register line only, no note). For us it was a factor of the E73 fine-tuning study of the route-conditioned head (K70): interpolating the clean-trained E60 head with a fine-tuned run (DEV 0.8123) was worse than the plain fine-tuned heads (about 0.825), since E60 never saw corrupted features. Head fine-tuning only, no link to the frozen foundation. Context: tried, negative, no next step.

Shows that full fine-tuning can distort pretrained features out of distribution (about -7 % against a linear probe), while fitting the head first and then fine-tuning (LP-FT) gains about +10 % out of distribution; image classification, abstract read only. It would matter if we ever unfreeze the foundation's decoder: warm up the heads on frozen features, then unfreeze with a small learning rate. In E73 / E76 a map-trust probe fitted on the frozen finished network learned nothing (AUROC 0.50). Watch: no action while the foundation stays frozen.

Averages the weights of several fine-tuned models (uniform or greedy) at no inference cost (register line only, no note). In E73 (K71) the uniform average of six map-trust runs was the best DEV model (0.842, better than every member) and became the v2 route-conditioned head, while averaging plain seeds gave nothing. It applies to head training, not to the frozen foundation. Use: adopted already; repeat it as a cheap final step when several runs differ in recipe, not in seed only.

Tunes only a chosen subset of layers, the best subset depending on the type of shift (first layers for image corruptions, later blocks for feature-level, the last layer for output-level shifts). In E73 (K69) it became the 'which layers' factor of the route-conditioned head: first block only scored 0.011 DEV below tuning all layers and BatchNorm-only reached 0.7861 against about 0.823, so the adaptation is not confined to the input stage. Head fine-tuning only. Context: tried, tuning all layers kept, no next step.

Radar pillars projected into the camera frustum give an occupancy map that multiplies the image depth distribution before BEV pooling; multi-modal deformable attention then fuses camera and radar BEV with aligned past maps. It was our first frozen foundation (K60, E15 - E24); E27 showed detection-pretrained features carry object evidence, not lane geometry (F1@1 0.624 against 0.867 for GaussianCaR), so it was replaced. It needs lidar-supervised depth and images, and no segmentation code was released. Context: baseline already run, no next step.

Camera-radar BEV map and vehicle segmentation: frozen DINOv2 image features, with radar points steering deformable-attention lifting. It is the published evidence for our A1 premise that radar adds little to lane geometry: lane-divider IoU 40.6 to 45.3, and map IoU 42.4 at night against 57.3 by day, radar lifting night map classes only about 3 points. Blocker: images, deformable attention and DINOv2 make it unrunnable on a cached raster. Context only: quote the numbers, do not re-run. TIER? evidence only, not a runnable baseline.
extract: skip: evidence already in the level-1 note; the frozen foundation makes its code irrelevant

text: Dense Prediction Transformer (register line only, no note): transformer features reassembled at several scales and fused by a convolutional decoder. In our chain it only names the decoder style of the frozen GaussianCaR foundation (K67, part of K61): a DPT-style decoder of 256 channels, whose output we cache as 32 PCA channels plus 7 logits. Nothing to port; our dense head is a separate small U-Net (K62). Context: no action.

CMX (register line only, no note): cross-modal fusion modules for RGB-X segmentation with transformers, which rectify one modality with the other before fusing. In our chain it only names the design of GaussianCaR's four-stage camera-radar fuser (rectify and fuse modules at 200 / 100 / 50 / 25 cells, 128 channels; K67, part of K61). Nothing to port: the foundation is frozen and we read cached features. Context: no action.

Lifts camera features LSS-style, pools them to BEV with a precomputed kernel about 40 x faster, and fuses them with a lidar BEV; map segmentation reads the fused BEV through grid-sample to each head's range and resolution. Map IoU is higher camera-only than lidar-only (56.6 against 48.6; fusion 62.7), background for lane geometry coming mainly from the camera path, and the grid-sample contract matches ours. The published fusion needs lidar, which we do not have. Context: no action.

Parameter-free bilinear lifting of a fixed voxel grid into camera features, with radar rasterised into the same grid (15 metadata fields, several aligned sweeps); vehicle segmentation only (C 47.4, C+R 55.7 IoU). It confirms that radar value comes from several sweeps and metadata (GaussianCaR does both) and that batch size and resolution outweigh the lifting method, which explains why heads on frozen features cannot repair a weak encoder. Needs images; no map layers. Context: no action.

States the stacking principle: a second stage must train on first-stage outputs for data the first stage never saw, because memorised data gives cleaner features than test data. That matches the seen-to-unseen gap of our frozen foundation (F1@1 0.93 on its own scenes, 0.82 unseen). Retraining k foundation copies is impossible with released weights, and the evidence is a graph-benchmark stacking paper seen through a search summary; the cheap variant is weighting head training towards scenes outside the foundation's training list (untried per note). Watch.

Lidar-supervised depth, a camera-aware depth module and fast voxel pooling for the LSS stream that CRN, RCBEVDet and HyDRa start from; BEVDet adds BEV-space augmentation. Depth quality limits camera BEV, but our foundation is frozen and lidar depth is training-only, so the block is unusable. One transferable lesson: BEVDet without augmentation overfits within a few epochs, and a head-side analogue (flip, small rotation, scale of raster and labels) is cheap to test, though blind spots make rotation only approximate (untested per note). Watch.

Four camera-radar 3D detectors summarised from abstracts: RCM-Fusion (radar-guided BEV encoder plus grid-point proposal refinement), SpaRC (sparse frustum fusion instead of dense BEV), CRT-Fusion and CR3DT (object-level temporal alignment, tracking). They show two design poles, dense radar-guided BEV against sparse query fusion, next to our Gaussian-set foundation. Detection and tracking only, no map or lane output, object-level alignment does not apply to static lanes, evidence is abstract level. Not relevant (out-of-scope).

Point Transformer V3 (register line only, no note): a point-cloud transformer backbone. In our chain it is the radar branch of GaussianCaR: a PTv3 U-Net turns each radar point into a Gaussian (K67, part of K61). The foundation is frozen, so nothing to port; practical consequences are that the model runs in FP32 only (README: the PTv3 part has no backward under mixed precision) and that its vendored folder shows no licence file. Context: no action.

HyDRa fuses radar pillars with image columns in the perspective view (height-association transformer) and refines in BEV with radar-weighted depth consistency; RaCFormer samples polar queries from BEV and the image view (abstract only). The one pointer for us is the occupancy output: radar helps dark regions (Occ3D night mIoU 30.1 against 25.8 for FB-OCC). Fusion sits inside a trained encoder and the heads are boxes, tracks and occupancy, so it cannot run on a cached raster. Not relevant (trainable-encoder).

Dual-stream radar backbone (point branch plus a distance-modulated transformer branch) and an RCS-aware BEV encoder, fused with the camera BEV by deformable cross-attention in both directions; detection only. Its useful part is the dropout test: losing camera views costs far more than losing radar, which supports 'cameras are the single point of failure' for A8. RCS-radius splatting is a cheap radar densifier, but our foundation is frozen and the paper has no map output. Context: cite as failure reference. TIER? detection-only, tier 3 fits.

Pre-trains a camera BEV network to predict lidar-derived occupancy and DINOv2 features, then fine-tunes for map segmentation; the map IoU gain is large at 1 % labels (20.1 to 25.4) and small at 100 % (45.3 to 47.3). It supports keeping a map-pretrained frozen foundation for our small training set (212 scenes), since ours is pretrained for the same layers. The paper has no frozen or probe experiment, and the pretext needs images and lidar. Context: no action.

Places one Gaussian per image pixel per camera by depth and 3D-offset heads and renders them orthographically into a 200 x 200 BEV; camera-only, lane-boundary IoU 47.4 and drivable 82.6 at 448 x 800. It is the design that GaussianCaR's camera branch extends with a coarse-to-fine depth, and GaussianCaR's map protocol follows this paper and BEVCar, so it explains how our foundation's lane layers were scored. Needs images; GaussianLSS was not read. Context: no action.

Bottleneck adapters (down projection, up projection, near-identity init) are inserted into backbone, view transform, BEV encoder and head of BEV detectors; adapters at the head alone reduced Lyft to nuScenes performance, and a geometric shift (CARLA extrinsic height) drops NDS from 0.666 to 0.313. Our shift is scene and location on the same rig, and the cache holds final features only, so inner adapters are impossible. Detection only; the head-only table row could not be mapped by the reader. Not relevant (trainable-encoder).

A coarse BEV map from a 'Driver' transformer is refined by 'Modifier' transformers that predict residuals at several semantic scales (road topology, then lane boundaries); lane-divider IoU 44.43 in the authors' own re-evaluation, with named limits: multi-lane intersections, rain reflections, long range, sensor failure. The multi-scale target decomposition is an idea for thin structures, but it needs the image path and autoregressive refinement stages inside the encoder, and cross-paper tables are not protocol-matched. Not relevant (trainable-encoder).

SpaRC-AD fuses camera and radar in sparse queries for detection, tracking, map polylines, motion and planning: the first radar-camera end-to-end baseline we found that includes online mapping (abstract checked in loop 14, register line only). It sets the expectation for A1: the reported mapping gain from radar is small (about 1.8 mAP) against larger gains in detection and tracking, so report both clean and degraded input. A sparse-query end-to-end system cannot run on a cached raster. Context: no action.

CRN-style radar-assisted view transformation and deformable fusion read out by a small two-level U-Net, with map IoU reported in 10 m distance steps (figures only: degradation proportional across classes, 0 - 25 m the safe range, night worst). The U-Net read-out matches our dense head (E17 / E18, U-Net kept) and a plain conv head loses only 1.2 mIoU; no per-range lane numbers exist in the camera-radar literature. Needs images. Context: the range-binned evaluation is a pattern to copy, no code to take.

Adds a segmentation branch and a 0.58 M-parameter detection-segmentation attention bridge to RCBEVDet; the shared BEV has 128 x 128 cells at 0.8 m and is upsampled to 0.5 m for maps, giving divider IoU 34.4 (not protocol-matched with the 45 to 50 of native 0.5 m camera-radar models). It supports keeping our native 0.5 m GaussianCaR cache rather than resampling a coarse BEV. The bridge gain is small (mIoU-7 42.9 to 43.5) and the paper needs images. Context: no action.

Lifts camera features into a polar (azimuth x radius) grid with the same cell count as a Cartesian one, so cells are dense near the ego and sparse far away; temporal fusion converts polar cells to Cartesian, applies ego motion, converts back and samples bilinearly (val NDS 0.496 to 0.509 from the polar grid alone). Our ego-warp by grid_sample is the same recipe (E41 temporal feature fusion, +0.008 F1), and the cell-budget idea cannot change a cached Cartesian raster. Camera detection only. Context: no action.

Learnable grid BEV queries attend to image features by deformable spatial cross-attention and to the previous ego-aligned BEV by recurrent temporal self-attention; detection uses Hungarian-trained Deformable DETR, plus a road and lane mask head (lane IoU 25.7, segmentation only). Its recurrent aligned BEV is the encoder-side analogue of our time recursion on vertices, but the queries are tied to the image encoder, so it cannot run on a cached raster. Not relevant (trainable-encoder); cited only as precedent.

Independent camera and lidar streams fused by concat, conv and an SE-style gate, so the camera stream survives lidar failure; robustness comes from limited-FOV and object-failure lidar augmentation (TransFusion-L under FOV failure 27.8 to 46.4 mAP). Staged training with a frozen first stream is our regime and failure augmentation resembles our synthetic failures, but we have our own failure series and A8 papers on gates. Lidar-based, detection only, projector about 1.5 s per sample. Not relevant (lidar). TIER? lidar plus detection only fits tier 4.

Image-based 3D proposals gather radar points by soft polar association (azimuth between box corners, adaptive radial margin) and a fusion transformer refines the proposals; no BEV raster exists in the method. Polar association beats Cartesian (AP 41.3 against 27.7), the same geometry as our ray and tip, but only as an analogy. Object proposals with hard thresholds, 4.1 FPS, camera detector required, nothing lane-like. Not relevant (out-of-scope).

CRKD distils a frozen lidar-camera teacher into a camera-radar student with four losses (radar, feature, relation, response); BEVDistill distils a lidar detector into camera BEV students with a Gaussian-weighted BEV loss plus a contrastive loss. Both need a lidar teacher BEV on the same grid and detect boxes only. One reusable fact: radar distillation does not rescue far range (CRKD 30-50 m gains only +1.03 mAP). Not relevant (lidar).

Sparse radar BEV features plus image Gaussian primitives initialised from radar keypoints, with dual-path temporal fusion, evaluated on TruckScenes in range bins up to 150 m. Its only value for us is the shape of a range curve: even this detector loses about 53 % of its mAP between 0-25 m and 50-100 m (36.5 to 17.0). The task is boxes for trucks on another dataset, and our lane centre-lines live inside +-50 m. Not relevant (out-of-scope). TIER? other dataset and boxes, tier 4 fits.

Each camera sees a wedge, so BEV is a polar (radius x azimuth) grid and every image column is attended into one polar ray; the decoder uses deformable attention with cylindrical reference points and Hungarian matching. Two small lessons: resolution decaying with range, and compute losses in Cartesian metres (a polar loss failed: 31.5 against 39.6 mAP). The encoder needs perspective image features and our raster is Cartesian and cached. Not relevant (perspective-only).

Encodes a whole road graph as a 19-channel dense raster (vertex score, plus edge score and neighbour offset for six angular sectors), decoded in one matching-free pass. Cleanest dense-to-sparse bridge between A2 and A3 and a possible fork and merge candidate source for the verified-ray builder; read, not run (K83). Blockers: undirected, world-fixed 60-degree sectors put both children of a fork in one slot, decoding is rule-based. Use: re-implement with heading-relative successor and predecessor slots, starting with an offline label audit.

text: Adds a dense BEV field (sign-free direction tensor, additive proximity, Laplace uncertainty) with closed-form targets, used to modulate features and steer deformable sampling. Closest published relative of our heat-map-plus-direction head (A2); its uncertainty gate is a principled 'better short than false' switch. Blockers: gains were measured with a trained encoder, the tensor drops travel direction, its confidence flags crossings but not small-angle forks, no code. Use: re-implement the targets as auxiliary dense-head outputs and judge at junction cells (K169).

Predicts semantic, instance-embedding and direction-bin rasters on the BEV, then vectorises by clustering, ridge thinning and greedy direction-guided tracing; no gradient reaches the heads and forks and merges are not handled. Ancestor of our dense head plus tracer (E31, E32) and the published dense-first baseline on nuScenes; it yields an estimated 95 vertices per 100 m against our 13.5. Code is GPL, read only. Use: re-implement its vectoriser in metres as a rule baseline, and try its direction bins as a multi-modal fork target.
extract: deep: code extraction later if needed

text: Encoder-decoder with skip connections for dense per-pixel prediction (no note, register line only). Our dense head is a 2.7 M-parameter U-Net (K62) predicting heat map and direction; in E17 it scored 0.613 against 0.493 for an FCN, and dense head plus tracer beat a matched sparse decoder (E31, E32). Nothing blocks it, it is already in the chain. Use: keep it as the dense head; any A2 change must beat it at equal ms per frame.

ConvNeXt V2 as an encoder for the dense head (no note, register line only). We tried ConvNeXt-V2 plus a transformer bottleneck as dense decoder in E18: 0.507, which is 0.11 below the U-Net, so the U-Net (K62) stayed. It touches A2 only as a negative result and nothing else is to be taken. Context: explains why the dense head is a plain U-Net; no next step.

Refines a D-LinkNet lane mask with a conditioned diffusion model (DDIM, 25 steps, started from the initial mask) before thinning and graph extraction; TOPO recall rises from 0.673 to 0.789. It is a mask refiner like our cascade refiner (E39, +0.001 F1) and could only sharpen the dense head before seeding. Evidence is 35 aerial tiles, undirected lanes without intersections, stochastic sampling, no code. Not relevant: aerial-only evidence; TP21 is the BEV version.

Reads polylines out of BEV masks: a query's mask comes from a dot product with BEV features and points from a column-wise soft-argmax, a differentiable readout; TopoMask drops Bezier regression for instance masks. It offers a gradient path from vertex positions back to the dense map (A2, A3) at low effort, but our position refinement and planner loss through positions gave little (E120, E121). Blockers: Hungarian training with real and virtual sets, per-instance masks, vertical lines, no code. Watch: soft-argmax readout only.

A diffusion model (ResShift, 15 steps, Swin-UNet) turns the ordinary BEV feature into a GT-lane-prior-injected feature before the CGNet decoder; on nuScenes TOPO F1 rises from 42.2 to 46.8. It could run on our cached 200 x 200 features (A2), but costs about 45 denoiser passes and three training stages, one host only, no code; our similar cascade refiner gave +0.001 F1 (E39). Watch: revisit only if a refiner shows headroom. TIER? never tested (K118) and heavy, tier 3 fits.

Predicts a raster map from the latent BEV grid with a parallel decoder, encodes it with a small CNN and adds it back to the BEV grid before the vector decoder (raster path detached); location-disjoint nuScenes mAP of StreamMapNet rises from 33.8 to 38.3. This is what our design already does (heat map and direction channels concatenated to the 39 features); an oracle raster reaches 91.4. The host is Hungarian-trained, so only the idea transfers. Context: outside support for dense first; no action.

Conv-RNN walker for lane boundaries on lidar-intensity BEV, trained through a 5-step unroll (softmax instead of argmax, Chamfer loss, ground-truth heading when a node strays over 1.5 m). It is the training-recipe precedent for our free-unroll tree (A3 / A4); E120 already has our Chamfer analogue, E94 the walker family. Blockers: merge is only a terminate (no merge edge), sequential single child, argmax at test, no official code. Use: port just the 1.5 m drift guard (effort S, register K161 first).

Runs an RNGDet-type agent (DETR-style next-vertex transformer) over a predicted nuScenes BEV heat map instead of image features, and carries the open ends of earlier frames as seeds. It is the nearest published baseline of our trace / builder family (K03) and needs only our dense heat map, but our E173 / E176 seed carry was a tie. Blockers: Hungarian-matched loss, about 0.41 s per frame, GPL-3.0 code, python-2 TOPO metric. Use as a quality-only baseline (effort M) plus the open-end-seed and tip-jitter ideas (S).

Vertex mask with NMS plus a small transformer that scores each vertex pair from features at both ends; SAM-Road++ adds node-guided resampling and interior / extension samples along the candidate. The standard dense-to-sparse link pipeline (K48); the pair head is small and MIT, and its set context aims at our weak junction recall J. Blockers: SAM encoder gone, undirected labels, NMS rule steps, aerial-only evidence; our link heads E42 - E56 tied the rules. Use: re-implement as baseline B2.

Predicts whole root-to-leaf lane paths with a MapTR-style decoder and rebuilds the graph by merging vertices within 0.15 m (Path2Graph), so no link head is needed. We take the Graph2Path labels from our piece graph for a per-path coverage and consistency loss (K12, nothing run yet) and re-implement TOPO / Junction TOPO as a report next to J, since no code is released. Blockers: Hungarian decoder on a trainable camera encoder, Path2Graph is only a distance merge, path sets are anti-sparse. Use: labels and metric, not the decoder.

Link score from a decay of the distance from the end of one lane piece to the start of the next, plus query similarity; the geometric part needs no retraining. It is the baseline of our link head (K30): E133 with the published width and learned heads E42 / E45 stayed inside the noise band, and its 2.8 m half-value is wider than our 0.5 m vertex error. Use: re-implement a refitted kernel as soft merge weight; expect a tie in S; no licence line, idea only.

text: Register-only (no note): Chamfer distance compares two point sets by nearest-neighbour distances in both directions, so no one-to-one assignment is needed. It is the matching-free loss family behind our E120 position refinement (vertex error 0.54 to 0.43 m), implemented there as point-to-polyline distance both ways, and DAGMapper uses the same loss on a free unroll. Blocker: none; plain Chamfer ignores point order and direction. Use: keep as the default set distance.

Register-only (no note): hard-concrete gates give a closed-form expected L0 count, so the number of kept items becomes a differentiable penalty. We use it as the vertex-count penalty and keep gate (SPF1 / SPF2) in the L4 branch runs E148 - E162 and in the E120e keep head; the sparsification review found no earlier use on lane-graph vertices. Blocker: the count term must be balanced against the task loss or it drives false stops. Use: keep as the sparsity penalty.

Register-only (no note): numerical coordinate regression (DSNT) turns a heat map into coordinates with a parameter-free differentiable transform that works at low heat-map resolution. It is the argmax-free way to read positions off our coarse 0.5 m raster; the register lists it only for the soft-argmax in E103e (pose volume), not yet for lane vertices. Blocker: none known; along-lane positions of heat-map peaks are noisy. Use: soft-argmax around peaks if vertex positions need gradient.

Register-only (no note): optimal polyline simplification with the Imai-Iri valid-chord graph and a shortest path, which minimises vertices where Douglas-Peucker does not. Our own count at 0.3 m on 60 test frames gives 13.2 vertices per 100 m against 14.1 for Douglas-Peucker, so the vertex floor is about 13, not 14.3. Blocker: validity of a chord does not imply validity of shorter chords, so the target can be non-greedy. Use: Imai-Iri path as sparsity oracle and DAG-merge target (planned variant M14).

Register-only (no note): Deep Snake predicts per-vertex offsets with circular convolution over the vertex ring and applies it iteratively, a contour-refinement decoder. The register names it as an alternative to our E120 refinement decoder, where depth and the gradient between layers did not matter (TEST F1@1 0.861 with 1 layer, 0.862 detached). Circular convolution suggests closed contours while lane chains are open and branching (my reading). Context: considered and not needed; no action.

Register-only (no note): DETR predicts a set with learned queries and bipartite (Hungarian) matching, the origin of the whole set-predictor family. For us it explains what we avoid: our sparse DETR-style LaneFormer (E32, 96 queries, explicit successor matrix) ended 0.058 F1 and 0.178 route F below the dense grid approach, and matching is barred from our losses. Blocker: Hungarian matching on the training path. Context only; no action.

Register-only (no note): PTDNet puts a learned keep gate on graph edges with an expected-kept-edges penalty (the sparsification review says two weights are tuned per dataset). In our plan it is the SPF2 keep gate for DAG-merge edges, listed in the hard-concrete branch runs E148 - E162. Blocker: the count penalty has to be balanced against the task loss, and no lane-graph use exists in the literature, so evidence comes from our runs only. Use: keep as the edge keep gate.

Register-only (no note): PolyWorld wires a sparse vertex set (256 fixed peaks) by Sinkhorn in training and by exact assignment at inference, and introduces count-aware scores (C-IoU, N ratio). Only the budget-aware metric interests us, as a template beside vertices per 100 m in S; the wiring is a polygon method with an assignment step at inference. Blocker: polygons, not directed lane graphs. Watch: an N-ratio style report could be added, no action now.

Register-only (no note): CoFi combines hard-concrete masks with a Lagrangian pull to a prescribed sparsity, so a density is reached by a constraint instead of one hand-tuned weight. Its constraint is listed for the SPF1 / SPF2 branch runs E148 - E162 (target near the Douglas-Peucker 14.3 vertices per 100 m; results from 10.2 to 20.0). Blocker: none beyond tuning; a count term can drive false stops. Use: keep as the density constraint.

Register-only (no note): a report that compacts ground-truth map polylines by Douglas-Peucker / Visvalingam, with more than 93% fewer points and AP still 97 - 100% at 0.2 - 0.5 m. It makes a simplification oracle an accepted training target, which backs our Douglas-Peucker reference of 14.3 vertices per 100 m. Blocker: none, but it is evidence rather than a method and is scored in map AP, not lane-graph quality. Context: justifies the oracle label; no action.

Register-only (no note), abstract read only: GLD-Road extracts road graphs from satellite images with global nodes and a connect module first, then a local search that repairs only broken connections (APLS +1.9% on City-Scale, 92% less time than RNGDet++). For us it is the idea of a repair step for parked dead ends in the E99 proposal, spending compute only where the graph is broken. Blockers: aerial images, abstract-level evidence. Watch; no action now.

A CNN walks roads in fixed 12 m steps (walk / stop plus a discrete direction); its lasting idea is dynamic oracle labels on states the CNN itself reaches, with a multi-hot target over all unexplored ground-truth branches. That slot label is a matching-free target for the b children of a tip, and its merge rule is the rule baseline for DAG merges (K14); not tried by us. Blockers: aerial images, argmax and threshold, one branch followed per step. Watch.

Grows a curb graph vertex by vertex, trained by DAgger: a restricted run follows the expert when the prediction strays over 15 px, then free runs follow the prediction, with the expert label computed afterwards as the nearest ground-truth point ahead of the learner. This is a matching-free label for any off-track state and could supervise the tips of our free-unroll tree (K50); dropping free exploration was the largest ablation drop. Blockers: aerial images, single-branch agent without fork handling, nothing run by us. Watch as a warm-start option.

An agent crops image features, segmentation maps and a raster of the graph so far; a DETR transformer proposes up to 10 next vertices with validity, trained by behaviour cloning on a BFS expert with a noised executed path. It is the root of the growth family we already tried as the E94 - E99 trace network (F1@1 0.851 on TEST, seeds limiting), and its label rules are covered in the CenterLineDet extraction. Blockers: Hungarian matching of slots, per-step image crop and backbone, aerial only. Context only.

Generates the lane graph as a token sequence: a DFS-ordered chain in which each step adds a junction vertex with its in- and out-links and a Bezier control point, decoded by a transformer from LSS BEV features (nuScenes landmark-F 56.4, reachability-F 67.8). It touches A3 only through its junction-level graph definition and the landmark / reachability scores, which the RNTR extraction already supplies. Blockers: quantised tokens with argmax or sampling decoding, vertices only at junctions, no code, camera BEV. Not relevant (TP23 duplicates this note).

A recurrent DETR tree tracker for vessels and airways in CT: a fixed block of extra queries per bifurcation, and the Super version trains over chained overlapping sub-trajectories so the carried query state learns from its own outputs, which removed duplicate branches and early stops. It is the closest published analogue of a fixed-shape b-ary expansion with carried state (A3 / A4); nothing run by us. Blockers: Hungarian loss, 3D patches, unclear gradient between sub-trajectories. Watch.

Hybrid road-graph extractor: candidate vertices from masks, up to 10 regressed neighbour offsets per vertex wired by mutual agreement, then up to 3 growth rounds from dangling ends (worth only +0.19 F1 over decoding). Only ideas transfer (reverse-pointing link score, keypoint candidate map, an oracle-seed test for the tree), with a tie in S expected; blockers: Hungarian loss, NMS, undirected aerial graph, dense vertices, no licence. Watch; run only the oracle-seed test. TIER? the deep file finds no module worth building.
extract: deep: code extraction later if needed

text: A cascade of detectors in which each stage is trained on the previous stage's output with a higher IoU threshold, so positives stay plentiful and train and test see the same distribution. The analogue for us is a tighter positive radius per stage (spec 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.3 m); it entered as the E39 cascade refiner (+0.001 F1, +0.014 route F, kept) and the E120 refinement (+0.012 F1@1). Blocker: IoU resampling between stages is discrete, so in a fixed-shape tree it becomes re-labelling. Use: already adopted (K42), keep.

Detects junctions, forms every pair of the top 300 as a line hypothesis, and scores each from 32 bilinear feature samples along the segment. It is baseline B3 (K40) for our ray verifier: a single-score verifier on the same teardrop ray, which an earlier review demanded, while E116 verified only junction / piece candidates on the learned graph. Blocker: both endpoints must be known, and one score cannot say where a long line stops being a lane. Use: run as a small baseline (effort S).

Volume rendering weights each sample along a ray by w_i = T_i * alpha_i, with T_i the chance the ray was not stopped earlier. It is the formal ancestor of our ray verification: alpha is hazard, T survival, w the chance that the last verified sample precedes i (K130). Writing the per-sample probability as exp(-sigma * gap) keeps it consistent when ring gaps differ; the mass of a ray that never stops is ignored and must be kept for censored rays. Context; not tried.

Iterative refinement of one estimate: each step looks up a window of a correlation pyramid around the current estimate, a ConvGRU adds a residual, and a gamma-weighted loss over all iterations supervises every step, with the estimate detached between steps. For us it is an alternative to the ring read (r = 4 cells on f0 / f1 / f2, 243 reads per query) and a matching-free multi-step loss (K07). Blocker: the window is isotropic while our teardrop is anisotropic; E94's fan and E120 already cover the use. Watch.

Each query reads only K points around a reference point at learned offsets over several scales, and boxes are refined layer by layer with the gradient blocked at the previous box. For us it is one grid_sample call around a tip (4 levels x 4 points); its fixed-fan, zero-weight offset initialisation is the precedent for a hand-built teardrop with zero-initialised learned offsets (K04, listed in E120 and the L4 runs). Blockers: Hungarian loss as published, unbounded offsets can leave the BEV. Use: sampling and init only.

Fixed line anchors pool the feature column along each anchor and an attention layer lets anchors see each other; the largest ablation effect is the line-aligned pooling (+11.8 F1 on CULane), and the anchor count saturates near 1000. It supports reading features along a hypothesised line, which our rays already do (K37, shared with CLRNet). Blockers: one x per image row and anchors from the image border, perspective images only. Context; no action.

Queries are dynamic 4-D anchors (x, y, w, h) updated layer by layer, and attention is modulated by the ratio of a predicted reference size to the anchor size, giving an anisotropic window; 4-D anchors beat 2-D points by 1.7 AP. For us it suggests a per-tip (length, width) gain in [0.5, 1.5] that scales the sampling teardrop (K05); nothing run by us. Blockers: Hungarian loss, COCO boxes only. Watch for a later teardrop variant.

Three DETR training tricks: look-forward-twice (the loss of layer i+1 also trains layer i through the undetached previous box), mixed query selection, and contrastive denoising with positive and negative noised queries. The first gives no-detach credit assignment in iterative refinement without sending gradients through sampling positions and is listed in the E120 decoder (K43); denoising is the DETR-side analogue of noisy teacher forcing (planned M7 denoising roots). Blocker: Hungarian matching for the main queries. Use: look-forward-twice kept; denoising still to try.

Lane priors are refined over three feature levels, deepest first, pooling 36 points along the current prior at each stage, plus a Line-IoU whole-lane loss; the code detaches the geometry and supervises every stage. For us it supports pooling along the current polyline per stage, coarse-to-fine with f2 first (+1.2 mF1 over the reverse), and a polyline Line-IoU as matching-free whole-lane loss (K37). Blockers: row-parametrised offsets fail for BEV graphs of any heading; images only. Use: re-implement the pooling and loss ideas (effort S / M).

Instances sample fixed plus learnable keypoints whose offsets are bounded in box units, and v3 adds a quality head (centerness, yawness) whose product with confidence ranks detections. It is the cleanest recipe for a teardrop as a reference pattern scaled by (length, width) with bounded learned offsets, and the quality head is a calibrated validity for the beam (K06, listed in the D5 / D6 branch runs). Blockers: bipartite matching; the camera projection is not needed. Use: pattern and quality-head ideas only.

The closest setting to ours: nuScenes map expansion as ground truth, BEV raster input, a Graph R-CNN proposes lane anchor nodes and classifies pairs as connected, with a separate direction net (93.5% direction accuracy). Its adaptive resampling label, projecting each predicted anchor onto the nearest ground-truth segment, is a matching-free loss that E120 already applies as point-to-polyline distance. Blockers: lidar + RGB + semantics input, one city, weak scores (APLS 0.176), no code checked. Context; our link heads E42 - E56 gave no gain.

First query-based centreline graph: a DETR-like transformer predicts Bezier centrelines from one front camera, and a pairwise MLP over per-curve association features gives directed connectivity, trained only on Hungarian-matched detections. It is the historical origin of the adjacency-between-queries link head that later papers copy, with connectivity IoU about 39 on nuScenes, and our learned link head E42 gave no gain over the rules. Blockers: front camera only, Hungarian matching. Context only.

Lane and traffic-element queries form a scene graph; a GNN passes messages along the previous layer's adjacency and an MLP scores ordered pairs (OpenLane-V2). In its own ablation the GNN adds almost nothing (TOP_ll 4.0 for the plain MLP head, 4.1 with the full graph) and breaks at three layers, which supports keeping our link head small. Blockers: Hungarian-assigned topology labels, set-prediction pipeline, front image for the traffic branch. Context; E46 / E51 gave no gain over the rules.

A PETR-style lane detector with two plain MLP topology heads; its message is that topology is bounded by detection: feeding the true topology to predicted lanes lifts TOP_ll only from 7.2 to 7.5 (R50). It also exposes a metric loophole (unmatched false positives with confidence 1.0 pushed TOP_ll from 7.2 to 19.0), a caution for A9. Blockers: perspective 3D position embedding, Hungarian labels. Context: why the link head stays small; E42 gave no gain over the rules.

Predicts lane segments (centreline plus two boundaries) with 'lane attention': reference points spread along the predicted segment, each head owns one region, and the first layer starts all heads from one shared reference point (32.6 mAP against 28.7 for single-reference deformable attention). Its BEV grid (0.5 m cells, 200 x 100) is a crop of ours and the reading matches our ray / ring sampling (K36), but our matched sparse decoder E31 / E32 was dropped. Blockers: Hungarian loss, mm-series code pins, labels only on OpenLane-V2 subset A. Watch.

A MapTR-style centreline-segment decoder with three additions on nuScenes: a junction heat map that enhances the queries, a training-only head that decodes the Bezier curve of a connected pair of segments for continuity, and an adjacency matrix refined per decoder layer. The junction heat map and Bezier-continuity auxiliary are the principles of our key-point head and connectors (E44 / E53: split / merge F1 0.34 / 0.38 to 0.71 / 0.64), so it explains rather than adds (K32). Blockers: Hungarian matching, 50 queries on 30 x 60 m. Context.

Each Bezier control point of a centre-line query is its own deformable-attention head, backed by an instance-mask loss and a one-to-many decoder; it is also the only published camera-radar lane-topology result (radar adds DET_l +4.3 and TOP_ll +3.0 on nuScenes subset B). It touches stage B (curve-aligned reads, K36) and gives a radar reference against our own finding that radar adds little to lane geometry. Blockers: Hungarian mask-L1 matcher, radar fused inside a trainable encoder, no model code, Bezier cannot branch. Watch: radar data point and cheapest read-at-control-points pattern.

A Pix2Seq-style autoregressive decoder rebuilds the lane graph from unordered keypoint prompts in training only, so the shared BEV features carry topology at no inference cost (+1.8 AP_ls and +1.5 TOP_lsls over LaneSegNet). The mechanism is an auxiliary gradient into a trainable shared encoder, which is frozen for us; only a training-only head on tree node tokens would remain (M8). The two notes disagree (not suitable versus reuse idea), the loss needs quantised tokens, no code. Watch: test only if cheap, low expected value.

Makes the de-duplicated lane endpoints a separate detection target with their own queries, couples point and lane tokens by a distance-biased attention and a bipartite GCN, and averages nearby endpoints at inference (TOP_ll 28.7 against 23.9 for TopoLogic on subset A). It is the published precedent of our explicit junction and key-point head (K31; E44 key points kept) and of snapping near endpoints when the tree becomes a graph. Blockers: joint token decoder, Hungarian-type assignment, released code differs from the paper text. Context: idea level only.

Puts geometry into three places of a lane-topology decoder: an attention bias from endpoint distance and angle, reference points along each lane's Bezier curve, and a hard-negative relational contrastive loss (ablation chain TOP_ll 21.8 to 29.2, subset A). It overlaps our link-scoring work, where learned link heads and TopoLogic-style scoring stayed within 0.01 of the rules (E42 to E56), and its own ablation shows the fixed TopoLogic mapping does not stack with its geometry. Blockers: 300-query host, hard-negative count unspecified. Watch: contrastive term, if a link head returns.

Uses one query per lane keypoint (11 per lane) built from a predicted BEV lane mask and an ordinal embedding, scores links only between the last keypoint of one lane and the first of the next, and trains a denoising branch whose fixed adjacency target needs no matching (TOP_ll 30.8 against 23.9 for TopoLogic). Keypoint tokens resemble our vertex tokens; our heat map already gives the spatial prior (E44, E53 kept). Blockers: vanilla branch needs Hungarian, no licence line. Watch: take only the matching-free denoising adjacency target.

Treats a connected lane (end of piece i joined to start of piece j) as an object predicted by its own queries, so a link exists where a connection query matches two pieces; TOP_ll rose from 12.4 to 23.3 on subset A. It is the closest published relative of predicting a turning movement through a vertex as one object (K34, stage C), the opposite of our pairwise edge scoring, which added nothing over geometry (E42 to E56). Blockers: Hungarian query groups. Watch: idea transfers, architecture does not.

A DETR detector places keypoints, then an autoregressive transformer emits each polyline's vertices as quantised coordinate tokens; a second stage fine-tuned on its own predicted keypoints lifts nuScenes camera mAP from 40.9 to 46.0 (fusion 45.2 to 53.7). It explains why we keep token polylines off the training path: tokenisation and argmax decoding break gradients and a chain cannot branch (our teacher-forced tracer E94 reached F1 0.851 against 0.867 for rules). Blockers: tokens, Hungarian detector, camera IPM. Context: the exposure-bias gain is only a size reference for our cascade.

Models each map element as an ordered point set with permutation-equivalent groups, hierarchical instance and point queries and Hungarian matching; MapTR-tiny reaches 50.3 mAP in 24 epochs at 11.2 FPS on nuScenes. It is the baseline of the matched sparse decoder family that we tried and dropped (E31, E32: dense heat map plus tracer was +0.058 F1 and +0.18 route F better), and a fixed 20-point set cannot hold branching graphs. Blockers: Hungarian matching, camera lifting. Context: at most the point-level permutation minimum and direction cosine loss.

Represents each element as a piecewise Bezier curve with a predicted piece count and a loss on restored curve points plus a rasterised region (nuScenes mAP 43.7 with Swin-T at 30 epochs). It sits behind our Bezier connectors (E53, split and merge F1 up to 0.71 and 0.64, kept), and its piece-count head is a relative of our validity gate (K122, sparsification reference). Blockers: bipartite matching, IPM positional encoding is camera-specific, no branching. Context: curve-restoration loss and piece-count head noted, no action.

Renders a vector output differentiably (pixel value exp(-distance/tau)) and supervises it with a Dice loss against the rasterised GT, removed at inference; it also defines AP_raster, which reacts to small deviations (MapTR 24.3 to 31.2). A pure-PyTorch soft rasteriser at 200x200 is a direct graph-to-dense bridge for the open gap of dense-then-sparse gradients, for memory losses, and a sibling of our point-to-polyline loss (E120). Blocker: published use is per matched instance. Use: re-implement the rasteriser (K116) and try it as a matching-free dense loss.

Adds decoupled attention, a training-only one-to-many query group (each GT repeated 6 times), dense auxiliary losses and a centre-line class with fixed direction, reaching 61.5 mAP at 24 epochs on nuScenes (57.6 without the extra queries). Our heat map already gives dense positives, the BEV-segmentation auxiliary is what GaussianCaR was trained on, and depth or perspective-view auxiliaries cannot be rebuilt on a cached BEV raster. Blockers: Hungarian one-to-one and one-to-many assignment (E31 and E32 dropped). Context: no action.

Represents each element by pivot points of a simplified polyline, with a per-slot classifier that makes the vertex count dynamic and a dynamic-programming sequence alignment instead of Hungarian matching (nuScenes mAP 49.2 at 110 epochs, 5.1 FPS). It is the nearest published relative of our validity gate and vertex budget: a simplified GT (here Visvalingam-Whyatt, ours Douglas-Peucker at 14.3 vertices per 100 m) defines what to keep, and a linearity loss keeps dropped vertices on the chord. Blockers: one ordered chain per instance, no branching. Watch: revisit for sparsity.

Describes each polyline by translation- and rotation-invariant edge lengths and turning angles, adds an Euclidean loss on them to the MapTR loss, and uses geometry-decoupled attention (nuScenes camera 69.4 mAP with dense losses, 15.8 FPS). It offers a pose-invariant vertex-shape regulariser for our sparse graph, which we have not tried. Blockers: ordered chains only, MapTR Hungarian matching, no temporal part and no location-disjoint split. Watch: a small loss term to test if graph shapes look unstable (K123, reference).

Predicts BEV masks first, picks key points from the thresholded mask (strongest pixel per 4x4 window, then farthest-point sampling of 20), refines point queries there, and matches noisy queries to their own GT by identity (nuScenes 71.6 mAP at 24 epochs, 10.1 FPS). It is a published analogue of our heat-map-peak seeds (192 peaks limited E94) and of a matching-free denoising target. Blockers: mask queries trained jointly with the BEV encoder, Hungarian for the learnable queries. Watch: farthest-point sampling on our heat map as a seed alternative.

Block reference (K131, BB04) for the correlation or cost-volume block with soft-argmax, here in its first optical-flow form. In our block table it stands behind the rough localisation of the SD map against the BEV (E103e; the rule version is template ICP, E82) and the registration experiments E48 and E74. No note exists, so detail is thin: this rests on the register line and the block table. Context: PWC-Net and OrienterNet (K99) cover the block better; no action unless registration is rebuilt.

Block reference (K131, BB03) for bilinear grid sampling and warping at positions given by the network. We already use it throughout: the fan and cross-section sampling of the trace network (E94), warps of the SD raster (E103d and E103e) and the ego-motion warp of the memory input (E105). No note exists, so detail is thin: this rests on the register line and the block table. Context: it is the standard grid-sample operation, nothing to adopt or run.

Block reference (K131, BB14): the output is a distribution over the elements of the input list, so a vertex can point at another vertex. In our block table it is the merge pointer of the trace network (E94), and the block tables of E128 to E131 list pointer attention again. No note exists, so detail is thin: this rests on the register line and the block table. Context: explains how merges choose an existing vertex; no action.

Block reference (K131, BB04): optical flow with a feature pyramid, warping and a cost volume. It belongs to the same correlation block as FlowNet, used in our block table for rough localisation of the SD map (E103e) and the registration experiments. No note exists, so detail is thin: this rests on the register line and the block table. Context: RAFT (K07) already covers the look-up-and-update pattern in the builder and OrienterNet (K99) the localisation; no action.

Block reference (K131, BB17): conditioning and gating, where one stream scales or shifts another. In our block table it stands behind the map channels as input to the dense head (E78), the gated fusion of SD-map tokens into vertex tokens (E104) and the route and trust conditioning series (E60, E75, E76). No note exists, so detail is thin: this rests on the register line and the block table. Context: explains the gated residual of the route head; no action.

Block reference (K131) for permutation-invariant attention over sets; our block table lists it under self-attention (BB11) next to Transformer and ViT. That block is already used in the edge transformer (E83 and E87), the trace blocks (E94) and the vertex graph transformer (E103c). No note exists, so detail is thin: the register line says nothing about induced-set attention or pooling. Context: no action.

Survival-analysis review that the register lists as the source of the discrete-time hazard with right censoring (K41); no note exists, so note has little detail. The K41 formulas are now checked against the primary papers in the VS01 deep extraction, which supersedes the review for our purpose. Nothing further to take from it for the ray verification, which is already coded as a masked loss. Context: keep as the register reference only. TIER? tier 2 is generous, VS01 covers it.

SparseOcc predicts 3D occupancy from camera images by coarse-to-fine hard pruning: cells are kept by a top-k whose k comes from the largest occupied count per sample, with BCE only on kept cells. Our sparsification study took from it the rule 'over-complete first, prune late' (pruned voxels cannot be recovered), a vertex budget set from oracle statistics (K141), and a speed reference (24.0 against 6.3 FPS at equal RayIoU). The task is occupancy, not lane graphs. Context: no note, no action.

Register-only entry (K125, reference): the title says it revisits training and scaling practices of online vectorised map constructors; only the abstract page was opened when the id was checked, and no note exists, so detail is thin. Such constructors are camera or lidar set predictors with matching, so at most generic recipe ideas (augmentation, schedule, scale) could transfer to our small heads on frozen features. Watch: read the abstract and tables only if the head training recipe needs revisiting.

Register-only entry (K124, reference): HIMap proposes a hybrid representation for end-to-end vectorised map construction; no note exists and only the abstract page was opened. Other notes use it just as a MapTR-family host (68.1 M parameters and 9.7 FPS in SafeMap's table, clean camera-lidar mAP 74.3 in RoboMap's). It is a camera or lidar vector-map decoder, so no head, loss or training idea is known to transfer to our frozen BEV raster. Not relevant: note has little detail; reopen only if hybrid representations matter.

A global segmentation network supplies the start and a cost map, then a local hourglass sees a 64x64 patch and outputs a heat map of border locations connected to the centre, so several branches per patch need no assignment; candidates are visited best-first and joined by Dijkstra (Massachusetts road F 74.4 against 49.3 for the best VGG threshold). Same family as our heat-map seeds (E94); it supports heat-map-valued branch targets and confidence-ordered growth. Blockers: bag and Dijkstra are not differentiable, aerial and retina data, no code. Context: no action.

A ConvLSTM walks over vertices on a coarse grid with beam search (wall-follower road order) and keeps a decoded segment only if the integral of a boundary heat map along it exceeds 0.7; on the RoadTracer set accuracy matches RoadTracer with about 32 k instead of 271 k vertices. The heat-map integral along a candidate segment is a direct precedent for our ray verification (K02), and explicit vertex choice yields sparse graphs. Blockers: sequential traversal, softmax and beam over a coarse grid, aerial data, no code. Context: no action.

Generates road layouts by popping an active node from a queue and emitting its outgoing nodes as relative offsets, sorted counter-clockwise in training so no assignment problem arises; a new node within 5 m of an existing one is joined instead of queued, which closes cycles (SpaceNet APLS 74.97). Counter-clockwise child order is a matching-free way to fix output slots, a role our direction-indexed teardrop rays may already play, and the 5 m closure is a first dedup rule. Blockers: sampling, aerial data, no code. Context: no action.

A self-attentive decoder emits a road graph node by node in BFS order with a soft adjacency to the frontier, trained by teacher forcing; its StreetMover distance, a Sinkhorn approximation of the Wasserstein distance between points sampled on edges, needs no matching or post-processing. It is a candidate matching-free metric or loss beside our point-to-polyline loss (E120). Blockers: toy-scale 64x64 grayscale input, fixed node order, fails on cluttered graphs, no code. Watch: metric idea only, to be added to the evaluation library if a matching-free graph distance is wanted.

Given fixed candidate key points, an agent adds edges with a pointer network, fine-tuned by MuZero-style RL whose reward is the change in a weighted road-network metric, with Monte-Carlo tree search at inference (SpaceNet APLS 0.778 against 0.743 for the supervised model). Removing the tree search costs only about 1 to 2 points in its ablation, which argues that a beam pays only if the per-step scorer is already good. Blockers: RL and sampling exclude gradient through selections, aerial data, no code. Context: no action.

A GNN predicts the whole successor lane graph reachable from a virtual agent pose; a rollout moves the pose along the best edge and merges overlapping predictions with weighted, lateral-only node updates (Miami TOPO P/R 0.481/0.670 against 0.366/0.654 for naive aggregation). The aggregation is a ready recipe for tree-to-DAG merging and time fusion, and its sub-graph with terminal scores echoes our per-level children plus rescoring. Blockers: Dijkstra pruning and merge rules are discrete, aerial crops, single-step supervision, code unreachable. Watch: aggregation recipe for the merge stage.

No network is trained for the graph: a road mask is covered by cubic-Bezier edges rendered differentiably and optimised per image, with discrete add, merge, split and prune operators (SpaceNet TOPO-F1 84.58; 14.0 edges per km against 52.2 for GT). The node merge, T-junction split and collinear merge are a ready operator set for our tree-to-DAG step, and its coverage loss is a cousin of the point-to-polyline refinement E120 (+0.012 F1@1). Blockers: 300 optimisation steps per image, DiffVG CUDA dependency, aerial, no code. Watch: operators only, not real time.

Each next move is one point that encodes direction and a flexible step length, guided by jointly trained road-segmentation and junction cues (APLS 65.69 on the RoadTracer set, second-hand). Our trace network already uses a step class of 2, 4 or 6 m plus a residual (E94), the same idea in discrete form. Blockers: the method section was not readable (PDF only), aerial data, training details unconfirmed. Not relevant: note has little detail, nothing to adopt beyond what E94 has.

The feature pyramid network picks the pyramid level for a region from its size, k = floor(k0 + log2(sqrt(wh)/224)) (RPN AR1k 56.3 for the full pyramid against 48.3 for C4). Our trace network reads a pyramid f0, f1, f2 with a fixed assignment (E94); the rule could be remapped to ring spacing or tip uncertainty, a distance-from-ego mapping no paper uses for centre-lines. Blockers: evidence is object detection, the gain for lanes is unknown. Watch: cheap ablation if the pyramid read becomes a bottleneck.

A recurrent cell emits a conditional hazard per time slot, and a survival-status cross-entropy at the observed time supervises the whole range before the event, giving denser gradients than the event-time likelihood alone (C-index 0.774, 0.892, 0.911 on three non-spatial sets). Our per-ring on-lane labels already act as the status loss of the ray hazard, so the new element is only an optional recurrence along the ring index. Blockers: no spatial evidence, no variant tried. Watch: a small GRU over the rings if the hazards look independent.

Represents an instance mask as a centre plus 36 rays with regressed lengths, trained by a Polar IoU loss (sum of minima over sum of maxima) without Hungarian matching; going from 18 to 36 rays gained 1.5 AP and 72 added nothing on COCO. It is the evidence for the ray count and for a scale-free ratio loss behind our teardrop ray pattern, which uses 12 rays, below the smallest count tested. Blockers: closed star-shaped targets, while a lane graph is open and branching. Context: no action.

A 4-D attraction field proposes line segments directly (about 4 k per image against 22 k for L-CNN) and the same line-of-interest verification head checks them, with both endpoints required to match junction proposals (msAP 65.7 against 62.9 for retrained L-CNN, 29.5 against 15.6 FPS). It supports giving the verifier informative direction-based proposals, as our teardrop does before ray verification; the head itself is unchanged from L-CNN (VS12). Blockers: junction NMS and matching, images rather than BEV rasters. Context: no action.

UFLD classifies, per lane and predefined image row, which grid cell the lane crosses, with an extra 'no lane' class, and adds a second-order smoothness loss on softmax-expected positions. For us the 'no lane' class is a per-sample termination signal and the smoothness loss a cheap matching-free polyline regulariser; nothing similar was tried. Blocker: it needs a monotone row axis, so BEV lanes of any heading, forks and loops do not fit. Context only, no action.

Sparse R-CNN replaces the region proposal network by 100 learnable proposal boxes and features refined over 6 stages by an instance-conditioned dynamic head, with box gradient blocked between stages. Its only use for us is the COCO evidence that a few stages saturate and that the starting boxes hardly matter (centre, image, grid, random within 1.3 AP); the matched sparse decoder family was already dropped (E31 / E32). Blocker: Hungarian matching on image boxes. Not relevant; no action.

ELSD describes a segment by midpoint, angle and length and scores it only by a Gaussian midpoint heat map times a 'line-centerness' ratio (min over max of the two end distances), with no sampling or verification along the line. It is the counter-position to our verified rays: with LETR and ScaleLSD it shows line detectors dropping sampled verification once proposals are informative, and the centerness ratio is a cheap centred-ness prior. Image line segments (Wireframe), nothing tried in our runs. Context; no action.

CondLaneNet detects each lane at its start point on a heat map, generates a dynamic convolution kernel there that yields the row-wise shape, predicts the extent as a per-row 'lane passes this row' bit, and lets a recurrent module with continue / stop states emit several lanes (forks) from one start point. It relates to our end and fork events (E94) and to the extent synthesis VS44, but its row bits and stops are non-cumulative decisions. Blocker: one x per image row, perspective images. Context only.

PonderNet trains a per-step halting probability with the expected task loss under the stop law plus a KL term to a geometric prior, so every stop candidate gets gradient and no argmax is needed; the stop law is the same hazard algebra as our ray verification (K41). We could use an expected endpoint loss, a length prior against early stopping and leftover mass as censoring; not tried. Caveat: expected-loss training spreads mass, so a sharp endpoint needs calibration. Watch; try next to K41.

The Mip-NeRF 360 distortion regulariser penalises spread-out ray weights (weight 0.01) so that mass collapses into one short interval, plus a stop-gradient proposal loss. For us it would regularise the endpoint law P(k) against the bimodal 'hop to the neighbouring lane' failure, with distances normalised to 24 m on our non-uniform rings; not tried. Blocker: it also penalises genuine bimodality, i.e. a fork inside one ray, so it is only sensible if forks have separate rays. Watch; no action now.

DAT bounds the offsets of its deformable attention with a scaled tanh (s = 2), predicted by a 5x5 depthwise conv plus a 1x1 conv, so sampling stays local. For us it is a one-line pattern for bounded read or step offsets, offset = r_max times tanh(.) with r_max a fraction of the ring gap; not tried. Evidence is thin: no ablation of the bound (only a stable sweep of s) and the task is ImageNet classification. Context only, no action.

BezierLaneNet models a lane as one cubic Bezier curve (4 control points), compares 100 points sampled at uniform t with the ground truth in an L1 loss, and samples through a precomputed Bernstein matrix (LLAMAS F1 95.17, 213 FPS with R18). The Bernstein matrix is the cheapest differentiable curve resampler and sampled-point L1 is matching-free once t fixes the correspondence, but we already use Bezier connectors (E53). Blockers: one cubic cannot cover a 24 m branch with a bend and a fork, and assignment is Hungarian. Context only.

GANet predicts lane keypoints on a Gaussian confidence map, each with an offset to its lane's start point, so keypoints group into lanes in parallel without Hungarian (only an auxiliary aggregation loss uses it), and a lane-aware aggregator reads 9 neighbours along the lane. 'Offset to a lane-level anchor' is a way to group sampled points into instances, close in spirit to our learned link heads, which stayed within 0.01 of the rules (E42 / E45). Blocker: a lane graph has several starts per path. Context only.

CurveFormer makes each query a 3-D curve whose position is an ordered set of anchor points at 10 fixed Y positions, projects them into multi-scale perspective features and reads them by deformable attention, with an explicit flag for points outside a feature level (OpenLane F-score 50.5). Only the ordered-anchor query and the in-range flag could be borrowed, and nothing like it was tried here. Blockers: monocular perspective features, camera projection and Hungarian matching. Not relevant.

DeepLSD predicts a distance field and an angle field and verifies each candidate line by the fraction of 50 samples whose field values agree (distance below 1.5, angle within 20 degrees). For us this is a free, non-learned verifier of a ray against our dense head (heat map plus two direction channels): a training-free baseline and sanity check for the learned ray verifier; not tried. Caveat: the inlier-fraction threshold is a hard decision, so baseline only. Use as the simple baseline in the ray-verification comparison.

Anchor3DLane puts 3-D line anchors (a yaw / pitch fan of 119 rays per start x, denser near zero yaw) on the ground, projects them into the front-view feature map, regresses x, z and per-point visibility and re-projects; two to three re-sampling iterations gain +1.5 / +2.2 F1 on OpenLane. It is a published precedent for a non-uniform, forward-dense angular fan like our ray fan, with visibility trained by L1; nothing tried. Blocker: perspective features (on our cached BEV the projection is a plain grid_sample). Context only.

LATR forms lane queries as the broadcast sum of a lane embedding and a per-point embedding, and replaces the BEV transform by a dynamic ground-plane positional embedding on perspective features (OpenLane F1 61.9; lane x point queries 70.4 vs lane-only 66.5 in the ablation). Only the factorised lane x point queries and the per-point visibility BCE could be borrowed; nothing like it was tried. Blockers: monocular camera model, perspective features and dice-based bipartite matching. Not relevant.

RenderOcc trains an occupancy volume with 2D labels only, by volume-rendering semantics and depth along camera rays (alpha and transmittance chain), adding rays from adjacent frames and importance weights on which rays enter the loss (Occ3D mIoU 23.93). The ray chain is a survival-type form like our ray verification, and the ray weighting and the distortion regulariser (VS07) are the only transferable parts; nothing tried. Blocker: it needs camera rays and a 3-D density field, while our cached BEV has no depth axis. Not relevant (occupancy, out of scope).

BezierFormer makes each query a cubic Bezier curve and applies deformable attention at five reference points spread along it, assigns by SimOTA top-1 (no Hungarian) and regresses with a Chamfer IoU on sampled points. Its ablations are the strongest evidence found for curve-aligned multi-point reads (five reference points over one: +1.5 / +1.7 F1), and Chamfer IoU is close to our point-to-polyline loss (E120). Blocker: a cubic Bezier cannot represent a branching ray, and the hosts are image lane detectors. Watch; consider for the refinement reads.

Polar R-CNN lets every lattice point of a coarse feature map propose its nearest lane in polar form (radius, angle), so about 20 anchors reach the second stage instead of 192, and removes NMS with an O2O branch whose stop-gradient is essential (CULane F1@50 71.68 to 80.81). For us it is a possible tip / seed generator (our E94 seeds are heat-map peaks, 192) and a case where cutting gradients is needed. Blockers: the O2O branch uses Hungarian, anchors are image-plane lines, no code found. Watch.

ScaleLSD keeps HAWP's attraction-field parametrisation but drops learned verification: a candidate line is scored by its support degree (pixels whose decoded junction pair matches it, minimum 10 in training, 5 at inference), trained self-supervised on over 10 M images (HPatches Rep-5 0.367 vs 0.322 for HAWPv3). It is evidence that agreement with dense fields can replace a learned verifier, supporting the free ray verifier of DeepLSD (VS14); nothing tried. Blocker: image line segments, pseudo-labelling at scale. Context only.

DeepHit outputs one softmax over all (event, time) cells instead of a hazard per interval, trained with a log-likelihood that gives a censored case the mass after its censoring time, plus a pairwise ranking loss. For us it is the PMF alternative to the hazard form of the ray endpoint law: P(k) without a product, but with no per-sample reading, and Kvamme and Borgan (VS01) report it slightly worse than the logistic hazard. The paper itself was not opened, only code pages. Context only; ranking loss not needed.

This synthesis card compares how lane detectors decide where a lane stops: a regressed length (LaneATT, CLRNet), a per-row existence bit (CondLaneNet, UFLD's extra class), per-point visibility (Anchor3DLane, LATR) or nothing explicit (GANet). None uses a cumulative survival product and none separates 'lane ends' from 'not observable'. This backs the novelty of our hazard-with-censoring ray verification (K41) and end event (E94); per-row BCE is the nearest non-cumulative hazard-like signal. Blocker: all assume a monotone axis and fail on forks; context only.

This card summarises three challenge-winning reports (2023 OpenLane Topology; 2024 Mapless Driving: LGmap, MapVision): gains come mostly from a stronger detector (big backbones, long schedules, ensembling), SD-map fusion, streaming-then-stacking temporal fusion and a topology head trained last on frozen detectors, not from a better link head. We already have the strong part (map-pretrained foundation, E27); transferable are training the verifier or link head last on frozen detections and resampling rare classes such as forks and merges. Blockers: ViT-L backbones, 16-GPU schedules, no code for LGmap / MapVision. Context only.

T2SG / TopoFormer adds an inverse-distance bias between lane end and next start to the logits of lane self-attention, plus a counterfactual layer trained on the difference between factual and zero-attention edge predictions (OpenLane-V2 A OLS 46.3 vs 44.1 for TopoLogic). The bias is a one-line addition if we add attention between vertex tokens (fork / merge candidates), but distance-based scoring gave no gain over the rules (E45) and the counterfactual layer adds only 0.1 to 1.1 OLS. Host is a Hungarian query decoder. Watch; no action now.

This paper builds the pair feature for the topology head from queries and keys of all decoder self-attention layers, so the link head reads relations the decoder already computed, and distils an SD-map teacher into a camera-only student (+0.7 OLS). It overlaps our learned link heads, where a node-conditioned head gave no gain (E46), and the paper's own extra-interaction experiment is negative (44.3 to 42.9). Blocker: it needs a decoder with N-query self-attention (Hungarian host). Not relevant.

RATopo notes that under one-to-one matching only a few matched queries carry topology labels, and adds topology supervision on a one-to-many assignment (3 predictions per GT lane) plus cross-attention before self-attention (TOP_ll with TopoLogic 23.9 to 32.2). It explains why matching-free labels are the favourable end of this spectrum: every predicted vertex can be paired with the ground truth through geometry, as in our link heads E42 to E56. Nothing to port, since the concept lives inside Hungarian assignment. Context only.

TopoEnhance re-scores node pairs with a GATv2 trained on ground-truth graphs corrupted by simulated false positives and jitter, and adds an edge-set Jaccard metric (TJS); after a detector it lifts TOP_ll (TopoNet 10.9 to 21.8). For us: train the junction / piece verifier (E113 / E116) and link head on simulated corruptions of GT vertex sets, as our learned graph has 1.8 x too many junctions, and add a TJS-like metric. Caveats: OpenLane-V2 hosts only, no code, TJS partly read. Use; test on the verifier.

ADMap fights point-order jitter in vector maps with a vector direction difference loss: the cosine between each predicted segment and its ground-truth segment, weighted by exp((1 - cos_gt) / 2) so sharp GT turns count more (nuScenes camera mAP 54.5 vs 50.3 for MapTR), plus a multi-scale neck and instance / point attention. For us it is a turn-aware direction regulariser for E120-type refinement (point-to-polyline, +0.012 F1); not tried. Blocker: it needs GT segments aligned to predicted ones, which the paper gets from matching. Watch.

MapQR runs self-attention only among 100 instance queries, then scatters each instance query into 20 copies with shared content and individual positional embeddings, cross-attends to the BEV and gathers them back (plug-in gain for MapTR 50.3 to 58.0 mAP2). The scatter / gather resembles our step token to vertex positions pattern and the decoder runs on cached BEV, but we dropped matched set decoders (E31 / E32). Blocker: Hungarian plus one-to-many matching as published. Not relevant.

MGMap adds mask-activated instance queries and a position-guided point-patch refinement: a 5 x 5 ROI-aligned patch around every predicted point on a densified mask feature is refreshed by attention and re-regressed (nuScenes camera Chamfer average 61.4, 11.6 FPS). The patch refinement is the point-level refinement idea of our E120 (bilinear samples at predicted positions, +0.012 F1), runs on cached BEV, and supports that design. Blocker: the instance decoder uses bipartite matching. Context only.

MapGR adds a whole-map loss: every query is mapped to a small 2-D map, all are concatenated and decoded to a BEV raster supervised by the GT raster with BCE, so unmatched queries also get gradient (MapTRv2 mAP2 61.5 to 65.0, FPS unchanged). For us the transferable part is a matching-free loss on the aggregate of all outputs: rasterise the output graph with validity weights and compare with the GT raster, which would punish duplicates and false vertices without assignment; not tried. Needs a rasteriser (VM32); no code. Watch.

DAMap replaces the hard label 1 of every one-to-many positive with a localisation confidence, exp(-lambda times L1 distance to the assigned GT points), in a distance-aware focal loss (MapTRv2 mAP2 60.4 to 62.8). For us this is a calibrated validity target: train the keep probability toward exp(-distance to the GT polyline) instead of 0 / 1, using our point-to-polyline distance and no matching; the soft-versus-hard target of the E120 keep gate (0.872) is not recorded. Caveat: the published form assumes an assigned GT. Use as one A/B arm.

Unconditional generation of lane maps: a coarse key-point graph is grown in DFS order, predicting each node's coordinates with a Gaussian mixture and its edges to all previous nodes in one shot, then a local decoder fills each edge with a curve (0.20 s per 200x200 m map). The key points then curves split resembles our key-point head plus Bezier connectors, but there is no sensor input, generation is by sampling, metrics are distributional, no code exists. Not relevant: unconditional generation. TIER? probably tier 4, generative.

LaneGraph2Seq writes a lane graph as a DFS-ordered vertex sequence plus an edge sequence of [child index, Bezier midpoint] tokens, decodes it with a transformer from LSS BEV features and applies classifier-free guidance at inference (nuScenes connectivity F 63.2 with R-50). Side facts: DFS order beats BFS, coordinate and random order, terminating tokens get lowered weights, and early termination is the dominant autoregressive failure. Blocker: tokenisation and sampling, so not differentiable end to end. Not relevant; no action.

Lanes become cubic-Bezier tokens (64 bins per axis) generated by a decoder-only transformer pre-trained on 3.3 M map-only scenes, with a flow-matching adapter that aligns camera BEV features to the scene tokens (OpenLane-V2 subset A M-P 45.6 against 42.7 for TopoPoint). Only the map-only prior over lane layouts, trained on partial graphs, could one day rescore children. Blockers: tokenisation and greedy decoding break the gradient path, the pre-training corpus is not available (no downloads without asking), no repository. Not relevant: tokens. TIER? probably tier 4, token model.

MapDreamer denoises one latent per lane under aerial-image conditioning with a cardinality head; SLEDGE generates a rasterised latent map with a DiT and vectorises it with a transformer, linking endpoints within 1.5 m and 60 degrees. Both are generative models for map synthesis or simulation, not perception from camera and radar. Small takeaways only: ghost padding for variable lane counts and the endpoint-linking rule. Blockers: stochastic sampling, aerial input, MapDreamer has no code. Not relevant: out of scope. TIER? probably tier 4, generative model.

LETR predicts 1000 line segments as transformer queries (two endpoints plus confidence) with a coarse-to-fine encoder-decoder and no sampling along the line (Wireframe sAP10 65.2, 5 FPS on a V100). Only the coarse-to-fine inheritance of entities is an idea for us; the matched sparse decoder family was dropped in E31 / E32, where the dense heat map plus tracer was +0.058 F1 better. Blocker: Hungarian matching and 1000 queries on image line segments. Not relevant.

Khurana et al. train an occupancy forecaster by differentiably raycasting predicted future occupancy into future lidar sweeps with no occupancy labels; the equations were read in the successor (Agro et al.), where the stop probability along a ray is the product of (1 - z_j) times z_i. That chain is again our survival algebra, and a 'virtual stop at the observed depth' for rays leaving the grid is a published censoring-like convention; nothing tried. Blocker: lidar sweeps and voxel traversal; the Khurana method section was not read. Not relevant.

UniPAD pre-trains a lidar / camera voxel encoder by volume-rendering RGB and depth with a NeuS-style SDF opacity along camera rays (nuScenes UVTR-C NDS 45.0 to 47.4), plus block masking. The only idea for us is sampling rays only where a label exists (depth-aware), i.e. verify only rays with an available lane label. Blockers: it pre-trains a trainable 3-D encoder on camera ray geometry, while our foundation is frozen and there is no pre-training stage. Not relevant.

Vampire adds auxiliary losses by rendering a BEV feature volume along its height axis into BEV height and semantic maps, with a Laplace-CDF density, to regularise intermediate features in joint training (nuScenes detection mAP 0.301). It is the only BEV-plane example of ray casting found, but along height and not along a lane; nothing tried. Blocker: it needs a trainable, height-resolved volume, while our cached features have no height axis and are frozen. Not relevant; no action.

Topo2D initialises 3D lane queries from a per-view 2D lane detector (20 instance and 11 point queries per view) lifted along camera rays and feeds 2D lane features into the topology head (OpenLane-V2 A: TOP_ll 22.4 with 2D initialisation vs 19.1 random). The principle of a good query initialisation corresponds to our seeds, and the matched sparse decoder was already dropped (E31 / E32). Blockers: perspective image features, per-view 2D detectors and bipartite matching; we have cached BEV only. Not relevant.

MapDiffusion diffuses polyline vertex coordinates (T = 1000, DDIM with 5 steps at inference) and draws 10 samples whose variance gives a per-location uncertainty map, 31 % higher in invisible than in visible areas (nuScenes location-disjoint mAP 35.6 vs 33.8 for StreamMapNet, 8.0 FPS). It is the vector-level case of the diffusion prior K118 (untested); the transferable facts are the sample-variance uncertainty map and a 3.9 mAP drop with a frozen encoder (31.7). Blockers: iterative stochastic sampling, 8 FPS against our 31 ms chain, trained BEV encoder. Not relevant.

GaussianMap replaces the dense BEV grid with 20,000 Gaussian primitives that sample LSS camera (and lidar) features, interact by attention and are splatted into a BEV feature for a MapQR + DAMap decoder (nuScenes camera mAP 70.5 vs 68.8).
