The splatting idea could turn sparse graph vertices into a dense feature, but nothing else transfers: it is an encoder-side representation with no radar, no temporal part and no code. Blocker: it replaces the BEV encoder, while ours is frozen and cached. Not relevant.

MapLightning drops the BEV grid: 1,200 learnable 1D map tokens plus flattened image tokens of the current and 3 past frames pass through a 4-layer self-attention transformer, then a MapTRv2-style decoder, with no camera geometry (nuScenes Near-Extrapolation mAP 35.3 at 18.9 FPS). It replaces the encoder our frozen cached BEV supplies, so nothing ports; no code released. Only its location-disjoint split protocol and the about 45 mAP ceiling it reports help evaluation (A9). Not relevant; TIER? the note itself says not_suitable, tier 4 fits.

rMCL adds a learned score head to multi-target winner-takes-all: each ground-truth element pulls only its nearest hypothesis, and a sigmoid score marks winners. It trains the b children of a tip without matching (A4, K38) and, by the extraction's reading, its raw score sum is a free fork-count signal. Blockers: evidence only for K>=3, a single GT continuation starves the second child, and the score means responsibility, not lane validity, so a separate validity head stays. Use: re-implement on the FC ring, test with fork scene T27.
extract: deep: code extraction later if needed

text: Discrete-time hazard network: one sigmoid per interval gives the conditional hazard, survival is their product, and a masked cross-entropy treats right-censored cases exactly. It is the algebra of our ray verification (K41) and already coded as the masked loss; no perception paper trains it with censoring. Deep file advice: floor convention at the raster edge, a per-metre hazard for the unequal ring gaps, per-ring calibration checks; limit: one failure per ray. Use: turn censoring on and add the calibration harness (toy test T26).
extract: deep: algebra only, the pycox library is not needed

text: Three generic remedies for the gap between teacher-forced training and free-running inference: DAgger trains on states the learner visits, scheduled sampling mixes in own outputs, DART injects noise into demonstrations. Growers in this cluster use them, and our E94 trace network is teacher-forced; the label function on arbitrary states exists from the GT lane graph. The note read abstracts only, and nothing is tried here. Watch: relevant when the time recursion or the tree is trained on its own outputs; effort S.

Straight-through estimators and Gumbel-softmax: a hard decision in the forward pass with a surrogate derivative in the backward pass; ReinMax adds a second-order correction at about the same cost. Generic fallback for any hard keep or pick decision in the tree (block BB21, K114, not used in training paths), but the gradient is biased and a poor surrogate can fail. A hard forward step also sits uneasily with our no-argmax rule on the training path. Watch: fallback only if soft selections fail.

Sparsemax and alpha-entmax replace softmax by a projection onto the simplex, so scores compete and unneeded entries get exact zeros. It would give a normalised competition over the b children of a tip, a differentiable soft NMS (K39, a soft-selection ablation). Blockers: one winner takes the mass whereas a fork has two true children (needs a two-hot target), a wrongly zeroed child gets no gradient, and no demonstration inside a training-time beam. Watch: ablation next to the soft top-k of MH34.

MCL and stochastic MCL train M heads so that per example only the best one is penalised: the gradient goes to the arg-min member, re-assigned every batch (sMCL, about 5x faster than the alternating MCL). It is the plain oracle loss behind our b-children training (K132): the winner-takes-all over b children is a min over b distances. Limits: no scores, so a beam needs a selector at test time, and with a single GT only one child learns. Context: baseline arm that MH01 extends with a score head.

Relaxed WTA gives the nearest hypothesis weight 1 - eps and every other eps / (M - 1), so starved hypotheses keep moving until their cell holds data. It is already coded as our mcl switch (share 0.1 for the non-winners) and is the baseline arm for rMCL and aMCL; E165 - E172 used it but confounded with b. Blockers: it pulls the second child toward the first (blur) and the bias is permanent. Use: keep as baseline arm. TIER? coded and run, so tier 2 fits.

GossipNet and Tnet learn non-maximum suppression from boxes and scores only: each detection is updated in blocks that pair it with overlapping neighbours and gets one keep score. It could rescore the b x M candidates before the beam cut as a set-to-set duplicate remover (K107). Blockers: trained on COCO for 2 M iterations, not end to end with the detector, and the gain is modest (about 1 AP). Watch: MH31 does the same job with a rank embedding.

Relation Networks for detection add attention between detections (appearance and geometry) and a duplicate-removal net that embeds the score rank; the best detection per ground truth is positive, the rest duplicates, trained end to end. This is our stage-C idea of sibling attention with a matching-free duplicate label (K09), and it is small (0.33 M parameters, about 2 ms for 100 detections). Label depends on the current scores; not yet tried. Use: re-implement as a learned duplicate stage against the rule-based one.

Modified multiple hypothesis tracking extracts airway and coronary centre-line trees from CT: template fits in a few directions, local hypotheses ranked, a tree of depth d scored by the average rank score, decisions deferred until a branch scores well. It is the non-learned counterpart of our verified hypothesis tree, and its rank score 1/R is a calibration-free alternative to raw validity. Blockers: not trainable, CT volumes, and tuning at depth 6 took about 88 hours. Context: classical precedent for deferred decisions, no action.

Stochastic Beams: Gumbel-perturbed log-probabilities make the top-k a sample without replacement, and inside a beam each child's perturbed score is drawn conditionally on its parent so the tree stays consistent. For us it could vary which nodes survive the beam cut across training epochs (K137). Blockers: it is an inference-time sampler with no gradient estimator, and it needs normalised child-given-parent probabilities whereas our validity scores are independent survival products. Watch: low priority.

Differentiable ranking and sorting by optimal transport: sorting as an entropic assignment between values and anchors gives soft rank, soft sort and soft quantile operators, differentiated through Sinkhorn iterations. It is an alternative to the soft top-k of MH34 for choosing the best M candidate scores in the beam, with the same bias trade-off of eps. Blockers: the paper itself defines no soft top-k (only a k = 1 loss), and cost grows with iterations x n x m. Watch: only if MH34 fails.

SOFT top-k casts top-k as entropic optimal transport of the scores to two anchors, giving a smooth top-k indicator with an implicit backward pass; in translation it replaced the hard top-k of training beam search. Most direct tool for gradient to dropped candidates: about ten lines on the M x b scores (K39). Blockers: dropped nodes stay partly in the graph while inference needs a hard top-M (train-test mismatch), and a loss must use the soft weights. Use: re-implement as the soft-selection ablation.

DiverseNet matches several valid labels to hypotheses independently and adds a catch-up term that always updates the hypothesis farthest from every label, so none is starved. It is the cleanest published form of b hypotheses with one or two valid answers and no matching, and the catch-up term targets our idle second child. Blocker: it pulls the worst child to the nearest lane point, so children turn redundant and need a duplicate step. Watch: fallback if rMCL and aMCL leave the second child starved.

DynamicViT scores token importance at several layers and prunes hierarchically; training stays end to end through an attention mask that blocks pruned tokens differentiably. For us the masking trick is the standard way to prune with fixed tensor shapes: dropped tree nodes stay in the tensor but are masked out of sibling attention and the loss (K136). Blockers: the note read only the abstract and summaries (ar5iv failed), it needs a target keep ratio, and it is an ImageNet ViT. Watch: masking idea for stage C.

PGP trains a policy over successor edges of a lane graph by behaviour cloning, samples traversals at inference and clusters the resulting trajectory modes (nuScenes, minADE5 1.30). Its edge policy is the same kind of object as our route probability on edges (A6, A7), and a route head could fill that slot. Blockers: the input is the HD map, which is our output, and sampling is not differentiable. Context: downstream consumer of a lane graph, no action.

H-DETR trains a one-to-one query group and a one-to-many group (every GT repeated K = 6 times, Hungarian on the repeats) in one decoder; only the one-to-one branch runs at inference. The idea for us is training-only redundancy, extra children per tip dropped at test time (K128). Blockers: it still uses Hungarian matching on the repeated targets (our rule forbids it), extra children multiply the tree size, and training costs +23 % time. Context: reference for one-to-many training, no action.

Co-DETR attaches conventional one-to-many heads to the encoder features and feeds their positives as extra decoder queries, each supervised by its own assigned GT without Hungarian matching; all of it is dropped at inference. Dense auxiliary supervision on shared features is what our heat map plus tracer already follows (E31 / E32: matched sparse decoder dropped, grid kept). Blocker: mmdet-style code, which our environment lacks. Context: confirms the dense-first choice; no action.

NMS Strikes Back (DETA) shows that IoU-based one-to-many assignment with NMS beats one-to-one Hungarian matching in the same transformer (up to +2.5 mAP); O2SFormer mixes one-to-one and one-to-several assignment for lane detection (CULane, 77.83 % F1). It supports keeping dense positives plus suppression as the strong baseline against any learned selection. Blockers: NMS is not differentiable, O2SFormer is a perspective-image lane anchor detector, and the note read only abstracts and a search summary. Context: baseline logic, no action.

aMCL replaces the hard minimum of winner-takes-all by a softmin with a cooled temperature: hypotheses start at the conditional mean, split at critical temperatures and end as plain WTA. This keeps both children of a tip alive early without the permanent bias of relaxed WTA (K38). Blockers: published schedules run 1,000 epochs, our budget is unknown, and with a single GT continuation the covariance is zero, so there is no split. Use: re-implement as the cooling arm next to rMCL.

Learned encoder-token selection: only the top-rho encoder tokens are refined, with the scorer taken from decoder attention (Sparse DETR, register K138); no note exists, so note has little detail. The one idea that matters to us is that the selection is scored by its consumer, which could inspire how candidate vertices are kept. Blockers: it prunes tokens of a trainable detector encoder, whereas our BEV foundation is frozen and cached. Context: background for consumer-scored selection, no action.

Supervised foreground selector with a cascaded keep ratio (Focus-DETR, register K139): tokens are kept stage by stage by a selector trained on foreground labels; no note exists, so note has little detail. The register states the principle 'over-complete first, prune late', which is a design echo for our candidate-then-verify builder, not something to port. Blockers: it prunes tokens of a trainable detector encoder, whereas our BEV features are frozen and cached. Context: no action.

DQ-DETR sets the number of decoder queries from a predicted object count (register K140, abstract checked); no note exists, so note has little detail. A count-driven number of hypotheses echoes the question of how many children a tip should spawn (short beats false), and the raw score sum of rMCL offers a count-like signal. Blockers: an image-space object detector and abstract-level evidence only. Watch: low priority, check only if the child count b becomes a problem.

Friman et al. track several hypothetical vessel trajectories at once so that low-contrast passages can be crossed; each trajectory is scored by a vessel template model that also gives the centre-line (coronary CT, 32 datasets). It is the nearest classical analogue of b hypotheses per tip, each verified against a template and weak ones pruned. Blockers: only the abstract page was read, tree and pruning details are not on it, no code was found, and no learning is stated. Context: classical precedent, no action.

Scheduled sampling flips a per-token coin between the ground-truth previous token and the model's own sample, with a decaying probability; free roll-out from the start is documented as poor. For us it would ramp the share of own children, not GT-nearest ones, fed to the next level from 0 to 1. Blocker: no gradient flows through the sampled input; not tried. Watch: if the tree or time recursion is trained free-running; GR27 has the wider toolbox.

Beam-Search Optimization trains a sequence model with the beam it is decoded with: when the gold prefix falls out of the beam, a margin loss pushes it above the K-th entry and the beam is reset to contain it. Its reset (insert the GT-nearest node when it was cut) and a margin on unnormalised scores such as our validity could train a tree through its beam. Blockers: a gold prefix must exist as a node sequence in the tree, and it needs pre-training. Watch: not tried.

Diverse Beam Search splits the beams into groups and penalises candidates already chosen by earlier groups, an inference-time change with no retraining (captioning oracle SPICE@20 28.09 against 27.34). It is a cheap rule against M beam nodes collapsing onto one lane, a hand-made NMS inside the beam using distance in metres. Blockers: selection is top-k with no gradient, and it competes with learned sibling attention (MH31). Context: a hand-rule alternative to learned duplicate control, no action.

Confident MCL keeps the task loss on the winning ensemble member and pushes every other member toward a uniform output with a KL term, so losers become low-confident on inputs they do not specialise in (CIFAR-10 ensemble error 8.75 % against 60.40 % for plain MCL). It is built for class posteriors and has no analogue for geometry; its loser rule would be wrong for our on-lane siblings, which are valid. Nothing is tried. Not relevant: classification ensembles; our separate child validity head covers the loser-score question.

Continuous relaxation of beam search replaces the hard top-k by k peaked softmaxes; the beam state is a convex combination of previous states and expected input embeddings, the temperature is annealed up, and a task loss reaches the whole beam. It is a template for pruning M nodes per level with gradient, but a convex combination of two positions is not a lane point. Blockers: averaging blends different lanes and cost grows with the number of soft selections. Context: MH34 gives gradient to dropped candidates more simply.

Polygon-RNN++ predicts polygon vertices one by one, fine-tunes with self-critical reinforcement learning on mask IoU against exposure bias, and ranks beam candidates at inference with a separately trained IoU-predicting evaluator. A learned verifier choosing among beam candidates parallels our ray verification, which sits inside the differentiable path. Blockers: the RL reward and sampling break our no-argmax rule, the evaluator is a separate second stage, and the task is Cityscapes polygon annotation. Not relevant: nothing to port.

Differentiable particle filters treat resampling as the beam cut of a particle filter: Jonschkowski stops the gradient at resampling, Karkus resamples softly from a mixture of the weights and a uniform with an importance correction. The transfer is evidence that training with and without the cut differs by a few percent (resampling hurt tracking, 79 to 75 %, but helped under high uncertainty, 39 to 42 %). Blockers: both are biased and neither discusses collapse. Context: background for the gradient-through-the-cut question, no action.

Beam treated as part of the model: scorer ranks neighbours, oracle cost-to-go defines the best, beam-aware losses trained on stop, reset (gold node back in) or continue (own beam) roll-ins. For A4 it is the clearest recipe for training with the beam in the loop: continue is our free roll-out, reset is gold-in-beam, and the oracle can be a point-to-polyline residual. Blockers: only partly read, no experiments seen, selection stays constant and node scores must be comparable. Watch; revisit when the beam cut is trained.

Two ways to draw exactly k distinct items with gradient: relaxed top-k (Gumbel noise plus k softmaxes, Xie and Ermon) and SIMPLE (exact k-subset forward by dynamic programming, conditional marginals backward). It would give a differentiable top-M cut of the M x b candidates (at most 100) in O(n k), the top open A4 item of gradient through the beam cut. Blockers: tested on feature selection, kNN and VAEs only, independent logits, and the subset law ignores geometric redundancy. Watch; try as a drop-in for the hard top-M.

Collobert et al. make a speech beam-search decoder (logadd merging of equal hypotheses, pruning) differentiable and train the acoustic model through it, keeping the gold alignments in the normaliser so the gold path never leaves the beam. The portable lesson for A4 is gold-in-beam during training; gradient still passes only through kept scores, as pruning is hard. Blockers: WSJ speech, additive path scores, effort L, and continuous vertex positions need a clustering rule for 'equal states'. Context; no action unless gold-in-beam is needed.

Evolving WTA updates the k nearest hypotheses per target with k shrinking from M to 1, so hypotheses do not get stuck between samples (synthetic CPI: EMD 1.89 against 3.94 for plain WTA). For a tip with b = 2 the schedule k = 2 to 1 is a two-stage annealing that overlaps with the aMCL and relaxed-WTA switches already taken in A4 (K38). Blocker: early k = 2 puts both children on one lane; evidence is synthetic plus a drone set. Context; no action.

Adds a set-level repulsion term: a DPP loss on pairwise distances, or pairwise mode distances used only in a 10-epoch fine-tune (Wayformer on nuScenes: diversity 57 to 74). For us a hinge on the child-child distance, gated to tips with two GT branches or to a late stage, could keep fork children apart. Blockers: at normal tips it pushes a valid second child off the lane, and from step 0 it destabilised training. Watch; test the gated hinge if fork children collapse.

MultiPath fixes K anchor trajectories (k-means), classifies the nearest anchor with a softmax and regresses a Gaussian offset only for it, so the mixture cannot collapse (log-likelihood 4.37 against 4.26 for min-of-K). Our E94 head is already an anchor-style classifier (bearing bin plus step class, teacher forced) and reached F1@1 0.851 against 0.867 for the rules. Blockers: needs K much larger than b plus suppression, and the hard nearest-anchor label flips at sector borders, where a straight lane lies. Context; tried, no action.

Kool et al. give an unbiased gradient estimator from k samples drawn without replacement (Gumbel-top-k, stochastic beam search): a Rao-Blackwellised score-function estimator with a built-in baseline, on a categorical VAE and a 20-node TSP. It is the only unbiased route found for training a stochastic top-b or top-M selection (A4). Blockers: needs normalised sampling probabilities and an episode-level reward, policy-gradient variance, and it is unnecessary while local supervision of the scores exists. Watch; fallback only if a downstream loss must train the selection.

Berthet et al. replace a non-differentiable solver (argmax, top-k, shortest path) by its expectation under random input noise, with the Jacobian by Monte Carlo and a Fenchel-Young loss that needs only the perturbed maximiser. A noise-based top-M cut without Sinkhorn could give a task-agnostic gradient at the beam cut, and Monte Carlo samples of a size-30 top-k are cheap. Blockers: top-k appears only as an example (no top-k experiment; CIFAR-10, ranking, Warcraft paths), variance with small M, smoothing bias. Watch; compare with MH38 options.

DeFCN picks one positive per object by a prediction-aware quality (class score times IoU, alpha 0.8) and adds a 3D max filter over neighbouring scales and positions (COCO without NMS: 38.0 AP, 41.1 with filter and auxiliary loss). For us the quality rule is a matching-free answer to which ray sample is the positive, and the filter a learned NMS over ray and ring neighbours. Blockers: labels depend on current predictions, the per-object argmax is a hard rule, Detectron2 code, image boxes. Watch; revisit for ray selection.

OneNet shows that adding a classification term to the matching cost makes one-to-one assignment NMS-free (CenterNet without NMS: 23.4 to 34.9 AP), and that a MinCost assignment, each target taking its cheapest sample, can replace bipartite matching on COCO. This supports labelling by score plus geometry without Hungarian in our sparse scenes. Blocker: MinCost failed on CrowdHuman, the warning for parallel lanes and junction mouths, where conflicts need bipartite resolution (the A4 gap). Context; no action.

Switch Transformer routes each token to the highest-probability expert, multiplies the expert output by the router probability so the hard choice stays differentiable, and adds a load-balancing loss against collapse onto few experts. The gate-value pattern matches our allowed selection with gradient through the chosen item, and the balancing term could serve as a weak slot-usage regulariser over a batch of tips. Blocker: forks are rare among tips (rate not checked), so a uniform slot-usage prior is wrong for the second slot. Context; no action.

Corenflos et al. replace the ancestor draw of a particle filter by an entropy-regularised optimal-transport map, so each new particle is a weighted average of all old ones and gradient reaches every particle (maze MSE 3.55 against 10.71). It is a way to cut a beam with gradient to all nodes, the top open item of section 3, shown on filtering, not on geometric graphs. Blockers: barycentric averaging blends different lanes into off-lane points unless the cost is local; O(N^2) Sinkhorn, biased. Watch, low priority.

Scibior and Wood keep the hard resampling of the forward pass and multiply each resampled particle's weight by v divided by stopgrad(v), which equals 1 forward, so the downstream gradient reaches the weights; unbiased for expectations under the unnormalised posterior. The pattern fits a hard top-M cut whose survivors carry multiplicative weights, with unchanged forward outputs, effort S. Blockers: dropped candidates still get no gradient, no numbers in the excerpt, learning the proposal is inconclusive. Watch; try on the survivors' scores of the beam cut.

SimOTA, from YOLOX, takes the k lowest-cost predictions inside a centre region as positives per target with k varying per target, replacing the Sinkhorn solver of OTA (47.3 AP against 45.0 for the multi-positive baseline). It would give a variable number of positive children per tip depending on quality. Blockers: many positives need NMS at inference, a non-differentiable step; the k rule is in the OTA paper, not read, so note has little detail. Context; no action.

DenseTNT scores many lane-aligned goal candidates with a softmax heat map, then replaces NMS by a learned goal-set predictor trained on pseudo-labels from an offline optimiser that picks the K goals with minimal expected error (Argoverse minFDE 1.27 offline, 1.37 online). Our ray-ring samples are the dense candidates, so it is a learned, matching-free replacement for our suppression step. Blockers: the pseudo-label optimiser is offline (not end to end), two-stage training, vector scene input. Watch; consider if suppression of ray endpoints limits quality.

MultiPath++ replaces fixed anchors by learned input-independent embeddings trained by hard assignment to the nearest component, and at the end aggregates many modes to few by greedy likelihood-weighted centroids plus EM-style updates (learned anchors minDE 2.305 against 2.99 for static). Per-slot child queries with hard nearest assignment are the cheapest WTA form, already covered by our rMCL-style training; aggregation matches our redundancy suppression. Blockers: aggregation is an inference-time clustering rule, no diversity beyond WTA. Context; no action.

DN-DETR adds decoder queries built from noised ground-truth boxes and labels, each reconstructing its own target, so those queries need no matching and early assignment instability is reduced (DAB-DETR 42.2 to 44.1 AP). It offers a matching-free signal for our refine and rescore stages and for a time recursion that starts from a noised previous vertex set. Blockers: it trains refinement and scoring, not generation of new hypotheses; the main queries still use Hungarian matching. Watch; try noised-GT hypotheses for the verification stage.

Wayformer decodes with 64 learned queries trained winner-take-all (closest Gaussian gets classification plus regression) and reduces them to 6 by the MultiPath++ greedy aggregation; the page has no comparison of 6 modes directly against 64 plus aggregation. It confirms the pattern of training many hypotheses and reducing by likelihood-aware aggregation, which is also the logic of our candidate pool plus suppression. Blockers: needs a large mode pool, aggregation is inference-time clustering outside the gradient path, scene tokens instead of sensors. Context; no action.

MTR uses 64 static intention queries from k-means of ground-truth endpoints; the query nearest the target is the only positive (regression plus cross-entropy) and NMS picks 6 of 64 (Waymo mAP 0.4129). Intention points correspond to a fixed candidate set in the tip frame such as our ring samples, trained matching-free; E94 tried the anchor-classifier form. Blockers: NMS is a non-differentiable inference step, and 64 to 6 contradicts a tiny b unless the pool is the verified ray endpoints. Context; no action.

Align-DETR trains the classification score toward a joint quality (class probability^0.25 times IoU^0.75, decayed by candidate rank) so that ranking by score equals ranking by localisation quality (50.5 AP at 12 epochs against 49.0 for DINO). It is a template for our validity score target: probability to a power times a closeness term from point-to-polyline distance; the paper does not frame it as calibration. Blockers: COCO boxes only, Hungarian-style matching still in the decoder. Watch; try the target on the vertex validity head.

QCNet and QCNeXt propose modes with a recurrent anchor-free stage, then refine with the proposals detached as anchors, trained by scene-level winner-take-all with a mixture of Laplace; Scene Transformer takes the minimum over 6 joint futures. The detached propose-then-refine pattern is the training form of our generate then refine cascade, and E39 (cascade refiner) gave only +0.001 F1. Blockers: scene-level WTA would couple all tips, which are independent; the README example needs about 160 GB GPU memory in total. Context; tried, no action.

DTPP pre-generates a tree of ego trajectories along reference paths, decodes every branch conditionally in one pass, scores branches with a learned cost and trains both jointly with a nearest-branch label (nuPlan non-reactive 0.8964; jointly trained 0.8948 against 0.8134 separate). It is the nearest published pre-generated hypothesis tree with learned scoring, and shows rule-based top-node pruning is accepted practice. Blockers: the tree is rule-generated and holds ego trajectories, not map elements; needs agent futures and the nuPlan devkit. Context; no action.

Villaflor et al. use K = 8 learned anchor embeddings as discrete behaviour modes, trained open-loop with winner-take-all and cross-entropy on the mode logits, then roll the one-step decoder out autoregressively with the mode held fixed and no retraining. It shows a WTA-trained mode slot can be carried unchanged over many steps, relevant to a child keeping its slot identity down the tree. Blockers: holding the mode fixed is an empirical modelling choice, CARLA only, no tree branching or pruning. Context; no action.

YOLOv10 trains a one-to-many and a one-to-one head on one backbone with the same matching metric, so the best one-to-many positive is the one-to-one top-1; only the one-to-one head runs at inference (COCO-S 44.3 AP, 2.44 ms; 43.4 AP with one-to-one only). The pattern (dense head trains features, sparse head picks one per object by the same metric) gives an NMS-free route for a ray fan. Blockers: image boxes only; a gap to NMS-based training remains for small models. Context; no action.

DiffusionDrive diffuses 50 of 1000 steps from noised k-means anchors, labels the anchor nearest the ground truth positive, trains L1 plus a BCE confidence per anchor, and samples BEV features at the trajectory coordinates (NAVSIM PDMS 88.1). It matches nearest-anchor positive plus per-anchor confidence on a nuScenes BEV backbone; the C20 and PL25 notes see a possible planner-path refiner. Blockers: end-to-end BEV backbone, about 60 M parameters against our 93 k consumer, one positive per sample (a fork needs two). Watch; only if multimodal planner paths are needed.

Rectify Don't Regret rolls a multimodal predictor out in closed loop: only the WTA-nearest mode is executed and supervised on the states it produced, classification stays on the teacher-forced sample, and gradients are cut across transitions (nuScenes collisions 3.95 to 3.08 percent). It is the only direct evidence for free roll-out with several hypotheses, mapping to continuing the GT-nearest child through the tree. Blockers: detaching cuts the path from the downstream loss to early children; trajectories, not graphs. Watch; candidate training regime for the tree.

DAC-DETR splits two roles in a DETR decoder: cross-attention gathers several queries on one object, self-attention disperses them, so a training-only auxiliary decoder without self-attention is trained one-to-many by a score threshold and dropped at inference (Deformable-DETR 43.7 to 47.1 AP). Our verification stage (gathering from features) and sibling attention (separating) play the same two roles. Blockers: the main decoder keeps Hungarian one-to-one, COCO boxes, and code reuse needs the DETR stack. Context; no action.

Ding et al. refine scores and boxes of SSD proposals with a graph neural network trained end to end, after a pre-filtering head cuts the proposals (abstract: more accurate and faster than other duplicate-removal methods). Same role as relation-network duplicate removal (MH31); it would map onto taking the best 3 x M candidates and a GNN over siblings. Blocker: only the abstract was readable (PDF text not decodable), no numbers, no code, so note has little detail. Not relevant for now; read MH31 first.

Group DETR runs K groups of queries through one decoder, each group matched one-to-one by Hungarian, so each target gets K positives in training and only one group runs at inference (Conditional DETR 12 epochs: 32.6 to 37.6 mAP). The transferable idea is K positives per target in training with one query set at inference; our earlier matched sparse decoder (E31 / E32) was dropped. Blocker: Hungarian in every group, excluded by project rule, and a tree has no query set. Not relevant.

El Khbir et al. cast graph generation as autoregressive sequence labelling and make training decoding-aware with a differentiable beam search against exposure bias (information extraction on ACE05 and CoNLL04). It is recent evidence that differentiable-beam training is used for graph-structured outputs, but only for text. Blockers: abstract only, the page does not say which relaxation or loss is used, no numbers, no code, so note has little detail. Not relevant for now; MH42 and MH50 are better described. TIER? tier 4 fits better: text domain, abstract only.

Kim et al. keep a tree of association hypotheses per track with online appearance models (2015), later pruned by a bilinear-LSTM gate (2018); the tree itself is not trained. It confirms the pattern that a learned gate decides which branch of a hypothesis tree survives, touching A4 and the time recursion. Blockers: camera appearance features on MOT16 and MOT17, non-differentiable tree, only listing and abstract read (PDF 403), so note has little detail. Not relevant for now. TIER? tier 4 fits better: appearance tracker, untrained tree.

Carries the 33 most confident decoder queries to the next frame, updated by a pose-conditioned residual MLP, plus an ego-warped BEV memory fused by a GRU. It is the primitive of our time recursion (A5); the BEV-GRU part is what E39 / E41 already did (+0.008 F1). Blockers: Hungarian main loss, the code's carry loss needs matched GT, fixed query set, GPL-3.0 read only. Use: re-implement the zero-initialised token update and warped-vertex prior; also run the split-overlap audit.

Treats online mapping as tracking: persistent element ids, a memory of four past frames chosen by travelled distance (1, 5, 10, 15 m), a pose-noised propagation MLP, plus a consistent GT and the C-mAP metric. For A5 / A9 it gives strided memory selection, a matching-free propagation loss and a template for identity-free consistency metrics; we only tried one memory (E41). Blockers: forks and merges not modelled, Hungarian for new elements, trainable BEV encoder, GPL plus non-commercial notice. Use: re-implement strided selection and the consistency metrics.

Accumulates warped local maps into a global raster by a hand-specified log-odds update: observation logit minus a class base-rate prior, weighted by distance from the ego. It is the only log-odds precedent for A5 (validity memory); a hard-gated vertex version already ran in loop 16 (E173, E176) and tied in S. Blockers: raster not vertices, offline and acausal, no clamp or decay, no pose-error test, no repository exists. Use: re-implement the six formulas as a soft, decaying, clamped fusion, first on the dense heat map.

Adds streaming to a lane-segment decoder: 66 of 200 queries are carried with a pose-MLP update and identity-followed forecast targets, plus prior denoising with an adjacency loss. The adjacency itself is recomputed every frame, not carried, and no code is released. For our recursion: sweep the carried share (their best 30 %, 75 % was worse than none in TOP), forecast loss on the warped prior, prior denoising. Blockers: Hungarian, fixed query set. Use: re-implement the share sweep first. TIER? ideas overlap VM01 and VM02.

Builds a global vector map: local elements are moved to world coordinates, Hungarian-matched to the stored map and merged, and a rendered map clip plus a 'traced region' mask is fed back into the BEV. For A5 only that mask is of interest (where the system has already looked), and VM16's overlap heatmap offers the same cue; our map prior at the grid is E40 / E48. Blockers: global pose, Hungarian merge, map NMS, drift not analysed. Context: why we keep no global map; no action.

Adds a Mamba2 temporal block to a BEV 3D object detector: four-direction scan over the BEV, history of 3 to 4 frames aligned by ego rotation only. It touches A5 only as a possible GRU replacement, but no latency is given and it is not shown faster than a GRU at 3 to 4 frames; tiny-model numbers are inconsistent. It is a detection model on a trainable encoder; MambaMap (VM21) is the map-domain SSM memory. Not relevant, no action.

Video lane detector whose gated Mamba2 temporal state names and fixes state contamination: the write is scaled by one minus the occlusion probability and a retention ratio is learned (flicker 0.052 to 0.024). Only paper found that models contamination of a recurrent state; the gated write is a small change to our spatial hold but needs a per-pixel reliability map (known in training, predicted at test). Blockers: image-space affine warp, perspective input. Watch: revisit with the loop-17 gate memory. TIER? closest paper to our gate memory (A8).

Compares three ways to use several frames for an STSU-type lane graph; the proposed one warps backbone features into a common ground-plane BEV and takes a per-cell maximum, and it beats merging per-frame graphs. Gain over one frame is small (M-F 58.3 to 58.8), in line with our E39 / E41 (+0.008 F1). Blockers: flat-ground homography, front camera only, exact odometry assumed, future frames used, Hungarian as in STSU, no code. Context: independent evidence that fusion adds little once a single frame is good.

Camera 3D detector and tracker that adds temporal instance denoising (noised GT anchors are propagated like real instances), a centerness / yawness quality estimate, and ID propagation with a carried-confidence decay of 0.6. For A5 it offers a calibrated quality head (K44) and a hand-made validity decay for carried items, both relevant to our open calibration item; not tried so far. Blockers: 3D boxes, bipartite matching in the noise groups, camera features. Watch: revisit the quality head if per-vertex validity calibration becomes the target.

Training-only add-on to StreamMapNet: the previous frame's GT is ego-warped, boxes are shifted and rescaled with noise that decays with the matched distance, and extra queries must regress the current GT; adaptive temporal matching picks the counterparts. For our time recursion it is a training source independent of its own early outputs, and ATM gives the validity target; streaming alone slightly hurt (59.9 to 59.2) until denoising. Blockers: box-level noise only, cleaner than real predictions, no code. Use: re-implement as a noised-previous-GT arm.

Feeds the previous frame's top-k vector predictions (k = 10) as queries, training on stored model predictions (real error distribution) with single-frame mode in half the steps; the unified version adds a map prior and displaces half the prior vectors by up to 6 m. Closest published analogue of our prior-from-previous-graph recursion; loop 16 already uses 10 % no-prior frames and small pose noise, but metre-scale prior displacement is untried. Blockers: Hungarian DETR decoder, global pose in the unified version. Use: re-implement the perturbed-prior recipe.

Keeps a global BEV raster (0.3 m cells) of the network's own past vector outputs, updated by an additive counter (+30 / -1, not log-odds), and feeds the retrieved patch back as BEV queries and decoder priors; night and rain gains are quantified, and pose noise (0.2 m, 0.02 rad) lowers 67.2 to 63.8 mAP. Overlaps our ego-warped output memories (E79 / E80 per the MapTracker extraction). Blockers: global pose retrieval, non-differentiable rasterisation (input channel only). Watch: only a rolling local window would fit; MIT code.

Adds to a StreamMapNet host a working memory of the last four warped BEV features and a temporal overlap heatmap that counts how long each cell has been in view, fed as a 32-channel trust cue (heatmap worth +1.7 mAP in the ablation). Our E41 fused features without any count channel, so an age or coverage channel next to the held input is untried and cheap. Blockers: no code, count unbounded and not occlusion-aware, no pose-error test. Use: re-implement as an age channel for the hold.

Memory bank of the last four refined BEV features and instance queries, fused by a gated diagonal state-space block scanned in four directions; history queries are re-ordered by Hungarian matching. An SSM memory is an alternative to our GRU (K117, not tested), but the only evidence is this paper and it runs slower than StreamMapNet (12.7 vs 14.9 FPS). Blockers: query reorder by Hungarian, code only announced, the linear-cost argument does not pay at four frames. Watch: revisit only if the memory horizon grows long.

Runs a slow stream with history and a fast single-frame stream over shared layers; small latent world models conditioned on the relative pose predict the next frame's queries and BEV (self-supervised MSE), and the fast output is used when the pose is unreliable. This fits our hold and gate memory and the synthetic pose-jump failures; trajectory conditioning hurt by 5 mAP. Next-frame prediction is untried (E41 only). Blockers: Hungarian, two forward paths, no reliability criterion. Watch: self-supervised next-frame loss on cached features.

Builds on MapTracker: each track keeps a stored BEV mask blended with the new prediction (confidence-weighted, decay 0.9) and warped by ego motion, plus a short-term future module predicting per-point offsets. That decayed, warped evidence is what our hold with decay (loop 16) already does, with a hand-set constant rather than log-odds. Gain over MapTracker is small (+0.8 mAP, 10.1 vs 10.9 FPS); it relies on track identities and Hungarian births, static lanes need no forecast, no code. Context: no action.

Training-only consistency losses: vector-level (past predictions warped into the current frame and matched, both directions, smooth-L1 plus KL on classes) and raster-level (focal loss between warped past masks and the current mask). Gains of +1.3 to +3.7 new-split mAP on three hosts, no inference cost. The raster part needs no matching and fits our dense heat map; temporal consistency is only a metric for us so far. Blockers: the vector part needs Hungarian, no code, detach policy unstated. Use: re-implement a matching-free bidirectional consistency loss.

A small temporal module trained on stored BEV embeddings with a frozen decoder: importance maps weight the history, deformable attention aligns it without an explicit ego warp, and the current frame keeps priority. Same recipe as ours (cached embeddings, frozen decoder) and the only paper scoring memory as a stand-in for lost inputs, but on simulated cooperative OPV2V data; more than one history frame reduced IoU. Context: supports a short, present-dominant memory for the failure cases (A8); no action.

Camera-radar 3D detector with recurrent temporal fusion: a motion estimator predicts per-pixel BEV velocity and occupancy, features are shifted by velocity x dt where speed exceeds 1 m/s, then fused with the next BEV; night mAP 33.0 against 30.4 for CRN. It is the only camera-radar temporal paper found and shows radar-camera history helps at night for detection. The velocity shift is for moving objects, not static lanes, the module sits inside a trainable encoder, and ego compensation is not described. Not relevant, no action.

One recurrent BEV state with motion-guided fusion: deformable-attention offsets predicted from current-versus-history queries align the ego-compensated history, plus a training-only heat-map consistency loss with stop-gradient on the target branch. Only concrete answer found to residual ego-motion error at feature level (A8). Blockers: built for moving objects, detection only, deformable attention over 200 x 200 is costly. Watch: if pose error is ever tested, a predicted flow field plus grid_sample is the cheap version.

Summarises encoder-side temporal fusion numbers: BEVFormer-S NDS 0.448 to 0.517 for 1 to 4 frames, HDMapNet map IoU 32.9 to 36.4, StreamMapNet BEV fusion +2.4 mAP, GaussianCaR only has radar sweeps as temporal input. It explains why our time recursion works on vertices and heads: encoder-side fusion needs retraining the foundation and cannot be added to a frozen cache, only head-side (E39 / E41: +0.001 / +0.008 F1). Gains are largest for velocity and occluded objects, modest for static map geometry. Context: no action.

A vision-language model (Qwen2-VL-2B) reads up to ten front-view images and writes lane vectors and traffic rules as tokens for 22.4 m map segments; points near a segment border are handed to the next segment as a map-rule cache. The cache is the only autoregressive-growth data point on carry-over between windows (cache off 41.24, on 71.32, but the printed column may be precision). Token decoding, perspective-only input and a VLM backbone rule it out, and forks and merges are not described. Not relevant.

Detector with a FIFO queue of top-K queries from the last frames, read by hybrid attention; ego pose, velocity and time gap enter through motion-aware layer norm (MLN) instead of a hard warp, and gradients of the first 6 of 8 training frames are detached. For our recursion MLN is a cleaner pose conditioning of carried tokens than a flattened 4 x 4 matrix, and truncated-gradient training is a template. Blockers: 3D boxes, velocity terms, image tokens. Watch: compare MLN with the pose-MLP token update.

Stores a global feature grid in world coordinates (0.3 m tiles), reads it by pose, fuses it with the current BEV by cross-attention and writes back with a conv-GRU; about +4 to +5.5 mIoU on several hosts, more at night and in rain. StreamMapNet took its BEV-GRU from it (our E41 analogue); our HD-map analogue is E40 / E48. It is a place memory needing precise global pose and repeated traversals, leakage-prone, useless in our scene-disjoint protocol, pose noise untested. Context: no action.

Propagates 3D detection instances recurrently: the most confident instances of the previous frame are re-projected (anchor moved by velocity and ego motion, feature copied unchanged) and concatenated with fresh ones (600 plus 300). It is the plain template of an ego-warped previous set, which our loop-16 recursion already does. Blocked by 3D boxes with velocity and camera features; the page does not give loss, matching or gradient treatment of carried instances. Superseded by Sparse4D v3 (VM06) and, in the map domain, StreamMapNet (VM01); not relevant.

Two training-time consistency parts on a MapTR-style host: a contrastive loss pulling the current instance embedding to nearby same-class historical ones, and a GT-free L1 loss between ego-warped historical grid maps (rasterised predictions) and the current one. The raster loss is a second precedent for MapTCL's matching-free part (VM23) and a repository exists (licence not checked); no consistency metric reported. Blockers: needs a differentiable rasteriser of our graph; contrastive part needs instance embeddings. Watch: if the VM23 arm starts, check this code.

Processes clips of three frames: 50 clip tokens summarise frame-level map queries, the BEV is updated by cross-attending to them, and an inter-clip memory of 96 tokens is read and written Token-Turing-Machine style (68.0 vs 61.5 mAP for MapTRv2, geo-disjoint 39.4 vs 36.6). Best published answer found to long-horizon memory with forgetting; our 128-d vertex tokens could play the clip tokens. Blockers: map tokens are DETR queries, about 2x memory and 3x parameters, 12.7 vs 15.6 FPS, ego pose ignored, no code. Watch: no action now.

Argues that stacking S frames gives the current frame weight 1/S so history dominates, and replaces stacking by a recurrence over one previous fused BEV with a learnable weight on the current observation, plus a sparse mixture-of-experts block in the tracking decoder. The single-state recurrence is the minimal feature memory we already ran (E41), and the 1/S argument supports keeping memory weight below the current-frame weight. Gain over MapTracker is +1.8 mAP; the MoE block is host-specific, ego alignment is unspecified, no code. Context: no action.

Gives each MapTracker track a rasterised history map, decayed (0.95), ego-warped and re-added each step, and defines G-mAP, a score for the merged multi-frame global map (MapTracker 49.4, itself 50.2). The decayed raster memory is the same family as PredMapNet (VM14) and our hold; the useful piece is G-mAP, a candidate source for the window-union consistency metric proposed in the MapTracker extraction. Blockers: track identities, perspective-feature sampling, no code. Watch: read the G-mAP definition when that metric is built.

Selects key frames by travelled distance (5 m stride) and fuses them by streaming or by stacking the warped submaps (mAP 54.0 plain streaming, 57.6 key-frame stacking), plus a soft geometry-aware classification target. Stacking two to four distance-spaced warped inputs gives long memory without a recurrent state that can be poisoned, the same idea as MapTracker's strided memory (VM04); the soft target suits our validity head. Blockers: Hungarian DETR decoder, no code, stack depth multiplies input channels. Watch: second source for the strided-memory arm.

Sparse map decoder with a query memory bank and a physical-prior denoising for polylines: four noise types on GT polylines (rotation about the mean point, common shift, scale, per-point curvature-based displacement) and no categorical noise. The taxonomy is the closest published model for perturbing a previous lane set when training our recursion; magnitudes, groups and assignment are not stated, we must choose them. Blockers: image-sampling decoder, matching behind the denoising targets unknown, no code. Watch: use as the perturbation menu for the noised-prior arm (VM02, VM03).

Predicts per-pixel offsets, covariance and confidence for the camera-to-BEV projection, then merges ego-warped past BEV features by confidence-weighted averaging (4 of the last 20 maps, chosen by position) before a learned temporal module; new-split nuScenes mAP 45.4 vs 40.3 for MapTracker. The merge is a non-learned feature-level relative of log-odds fusion and a second precedent beside L2G-Map (VM12). Blockers: the probabilistic projection needs camera lifting, absent on the cached BEV; MapTracker head. Watch: read the merge if a confidence-weighted fusion arm is built; a repository exists.

SuperGlue appends one learnable dustbin row and column to the score matrix and runs Sinkhorn: a differentiable assignment with an explicit no-match mass, trained by plain NLL, no Hungarian matching. It targets the missing abstain output of our route head (A6); nothing similar was run. Blocker: one-to-one marginals push the mass of many lanes of one road into the bin, so we need a row softmax with a bin column or capacitated Sinkhorn; code is read only. Use: re-implement equations 7-10, 3-way softmax as control.

OrienterNet correlates a neural BEV with an OSM raster over all (x, y, heading) via FFT and returns a pose probability volume that is fused over frames by multiplying volumes. It is our 'no pose given' front end (K99): explicit uncertainty, an abstain input, temporal fusion of the registration; E103e showed a volume works as a module but gave no route-success gain. Blockers: single frames are weak (15.8 percent within 1 m), memory, CC-BY-NC code. Use: re-implement a small coarse-to-fine volume on our BEV.

SMERF turns OSM polylines (11 points plus road class) into tokens with a 6-layer transformer and fuses them into BEV queries by cross-attention. It is the nearest published vector SD-token encoder for our route head, which uses raster tokens (E104b); polyline tokens were not tried. Limits: geometry only, no route, no pose-noise or wrong-map test, exact pose assumed, non-commercial licence. Use: re-implement, add a route flag and a null token, compare with raster tokens.

MAT (Online Navigation Refinement) assigns each perceived centre-line to one SD road by a softmax over pooled road tokens, with path-aware attention along the lane graph. Summing it over route roads gives a soft road-level route probability for our vertices (K75); lane level, a fallback and abstention must be added by us, and SD shift was never trained. Blockers: per-vertex road-id labels, 34-70 ms on an A6000, trained on ground-truth maps only; code is MIT. Use: re-implement the head on 128-d vertex tokens.

NavMapFusion adds SD-map cross-attention to a diffusion map decoder and sweeps map faults: 1 m shift noise, element dropout, wrong-map samples (10 percent). It has no trust or abstain output; a wrong map without such training is worse than none. Our map-fault training (E87) already covers these families but never drops the route polyline and has no family-by-family sweep. Model unusable (diffusion decoder, no code, GPL); use: adopt the sweep and a route-polyline dropout fault.

MapLocNet registers BEV features to a rasterised OSM patch with a coarse-to-fine transformer that regresses (dx, dy, dtheta) directly, with no volume and no uncertainty. It is the simplest differentiable registration head (K100), but only 20 percent within 1 m on nuScenes with six cameras shows that regression on weak OSM is crude. Our registration front end (E48, E74) is already kept. Blockers: camera LSS BEV encoder, 22.9 M parameters. Context only; no action.

TopoSD (no note; register line and loop-7 source table only) fuses the SD map into LaneSegNet as raster canvas plus vector tokens. A clean-trained model falls from 40.2 to 23.6 mAP under 5 m shift, a noise-trained one holds 34.6 but loses about 5 mAP on clean maps. Its noise recipe went into E78 (K73); the clean versus noise-trained trade-off was never measured on our head. Context; no action.

TrajTopo (no note; register line and loop-7 source table only) uses crowdsourced trajectory priors, not an SD map, with a spatial alignment module that predicts per-position offsets and a per-pixel softmax gate between sensor and prior features. On LaneSegNet AP rises 32.3 to 42.3 (alignment module +1.2); no noise test. Our E78/E80 head gates the prior only implicitly (K76). Watch: the gate is a 10-line module for the dense head; evidence is thin.

U-ViLAR matches visual BEV features to a rasterised map by a softmax association with a pixel-wise uncertainty map, then outputs x, y and heading distributions whose entropy is the uncertainty, refining the pose by a softmax-weighted average (no argmax). It overlaps our OrienterNet pose-volume plan (K100) and offers an entropy-based confidence for abstention; our correlation volume (E103) was dropped. Blockers: camera BEV encoder, no code found, no dedicated map-error study. Watch only.

HOLO replaces a full pose volume by up to 6 RAFT-style iterations of local correlation lookups around the current estimate plus a DLT homography; recall within 1 m is 36.4 percent on nuScenes with OSM. It could make a registration volume cheaper (19.9 FPS at 6 iterations on an A6000) if we build one; our E103 volume was not better than cross-attention. Blockers: camera BEV, code announced but unavailable, differentiable DLT not confirmed. Watch.

UMPE encodes HD, OSM, satellite or SD priors as tokens with confidences and fuses them by cross-attention with an additive log-confidence bias, a presence-normalised gate and source dropout 0.3. We already took the gate and source dropout (K98 in E87 and E104); the log-confidence bias is the soft form of our validity mask. Planning gain is open loop with VAD only, no noise test on the prior. Context for the gate design; the bias is an optional small port.

D2HDMap rasterises lane drivelines as a non-visible prior to initialise map queries and tabulates noise-aware training: with translation sigma up to 2 m and rotation up to 5 degrees, robust training gains 3.86 mAP on average and 6.9 at 2 m plus 5 degrees, yet mAP still falls roughly linearly with shift. Our route success loses about 0.03 per metre, a flatter curve, and map offsets of 0-3 m were tested. Host is DETR with Hungarian matching; no code. Context only.

SMART pre-trains a map-prior network offline on SD polylines plus satellite crops against about 200 k HD-map scenes, freezes it, and injects its BEV features into TopoNet or TopoMLP; SMERF is covered in PL43. The benefit grows with pre-training data (TOP_ll 16.2 to 31.9) but needs satellite imagery and a large HD corpus we lack, and the GPS pose is assumed exact. Our route head already cross-attends to SD tokens (E104b). Context (K52); no action.

SCORE stacks SD-map queries, one-to-many supervision, denoising, a distance link blend and a ConvGRU on LaneSegNet; the ConvGRU gain (about 4 DET_ls) has no epoch-matched control. The SD map only seeds queries: no route bit, no noise or wrong-map test. Not usable as a model (no code, mm-stack, Hungarian). Watch: a distance prior on the route score, and a 2x2 test of SD map by time recursion under offsets. TIER? idea-level only, tier 2 fits.

Deep Global Registration shows that a network can predict a confidence per correspondence and a closed-form weighted Procrustes then gives the rigid transform, with gradient through the weights. Soft vertex-to-road-point weights from an assignment head (C30) could give a per-frame offset in closed form at negligible cost. Blockers: no SE(2) variant seen, we would derive the 2-D form ourselves, point-to-point residuals suit curves poorly (E120 uses point-to-polyline); only the abstract was read. Watch; relevant only after a dustbin assignment exists.

GC-PGP biases lane-graph traversal with the route: a learnable additive bonus on on-route edges (soft) or zero probability for off-route edges (hard). The hard mask applied in training was much less robust to wrong route labels on nuPlan, which supports keeping our route probability soft and the hard step off the training path. Our planner consumer E117 already reads a route probability per edge. Evidence is nuPlan only and from 2023. Context; no action.

A matchability score per point plus a double softmax replaces Sinkhorn, with early exit and pruning; relative pose takes 44 ms against 70 ms for SuperGlue. A sigmoid 'has a road on the map' head per vertex plus row softmax is the cheapest abstain-capable assignment for the route head (axis A6 rather than A7); our keep gate exists for vertices but not for map assignment. Blockers: feature-matching setting, per-layer exit not worth it at our size. Watch: abstain head test in the route head.

EgoVM scores a grid of pose offsets (plus or minus 3 m, 3 degrees) by sampling BEV features at projected vector-map points with a shared MLP, and takes the posterior mean and covariance as pose and uncertainty. The sampling primitive is the grid_sample our trace network already uses, but the average run time is 120 ms on an RTX 3080 against our 31 ms chain, and we dropped a similar volume (E103). No code found. Background for a cheaper pose volume; context.

P-MapNet cross-attends BEV features to a rasterised OSM centre-line prior (2 layers best, 4 or more overfit) and optionally refines with an HD-map masked autoencoder. Its fusion ablation (cross-attention 60.20 mIoU against 56.27 for CNN concat) supports what our route head does with SD raster tokens (E40, E48, E104). Weak alignment is tolerated, not corrected, and no GPS-noise experiment is given; the HD-prior part is heavy and not relevant. Context; no action.

Bateman et al. train prior-informed map models on synthetic prior perturbations and test on a real 3-year-old map: the best synthetic recipe still leaves a gap (about 0.136 mAP between synthetic and real), heavily corrupted priors can be worse than no prior, and the model tends to copy the prior when changes are complex. For us it warns that synthetic map offsets overstate robustness; add a copy-the-map check (does the route head follow the map when the lanes disagree?). Data is private. Watch.

RAVE aligns map and BEV features by a correlation-volume flow, then solves pose in decoupled steps (yaw, then along, then across), which turns a product of hypotheses into a sum (96 percent less solver memory), and refines with a transformer only when the peak probability is below 0.4. Both tricks could cut a pose volume's cost and give refine-only-if-uncertain. But it needs HD map rasters, six cameras and about 150 ms on an RTX 3090; no code link; our E103 volume was dropped. Watch.

Uni-PrevPredMap trains one model with sampled modes (no prior 0.5, temporal prior 0.3, both 0.2), so a missing prior is a normal operating mode, and tabulates perturbations: frame shifts of 3-9 m (77.0 to 74.6 mAP) are almost as bad as an empty map (74.0). Our E87 already samples no-map and wrong-map cases; the empty-map floor and the displacement table are a reporting template. Camera detection host. Context; no action.

This paper decodes which road the vehicle is on with an HMM (road connectivity as transitions, GNSS plus lane-marking association, a scenario factor) and Viterbi. It is the classical, non-differentiable form of temporal accumulation over a road assignment (A5, A6); its log-odds form could in principle be fused with a learned route score. Blockers: needs lane-marking detections and GNSS, not our centre-line graph; no gradient. Context only. TIER? tier 3 fits: no K id, inputs we lack.

SDTagNet makes every SD point a query with sin/cos position, an OSM-tag text embedding and a random-feature element identifier tying the points of one polyline, fused by cross-attention in a MapTRv2 decoder; far-range mAP rises 13.0 to 18.9 on Argoverse 2. The element identifier is a cheap way to mark which tokens belong to one SD road if we adopt polyline tokens (PL43, PL01 pooling). Its authors report that noise and drop augmentation hurt, a counter-result to our map-fault training; text tags are heavy. Watch.

RTMap lets prior-map elements act as queries labelled map or outdated in training, so low confidence flags an outdated element, and gets the pose from an MLP or a least-squares step with covariance (lateral error 0.121 m on nuScenes). The per-element 'still true' confidence matches our open map-trust output, which the project approaches label-free with a map-agreement monitor. Blockers: Hungarian matching for new elements, camera host, change labels needed. Context; no action.

OpenLane-V2-OSM fuses SD maps into lane detection as a raster (about 13 M extra parameters) or as a graph with a GNN (1.7 M) and measures localisation error: rotation hurts much more than translation (10 degrees costs 13.6-21.1 percent, 0.25-2 m shifts 0.45-10.8 percent). For us the rotation finding says our map-offset sweep must include heading, and graph-style SD fusion is a cheaper alternative to raster tokens. No route is used, no code, Argoverse 2 data. Context.

NavigScene generates textual navigation guidance (Google Maps images described by GPT-4o), compresses the frozen VLM output and concatenates it with BEV features; Geo-VLA instead trains map knowledge into a VLM and uses no map at inference. Only the weak observation that planners gain a little from route context carries over (SparseDrive L2 1.01 to 0.76 m). Text and VLM interface, heavy compute, no lane graph or route attribute, unclear how guidance arises at inference. Not relevant: out of scope.

Rule-based planner: Dijkstra over route lanes gives one centre-line, 15 proposals (5 IDM speeds x 3 lateral offsets) are simulated and scored; Val14 closed-loop 92 / 93. It is the planner-aware test bed our chain lacks: swap GT, perceived and degraded graphs into the same planner; the project has no rule-based consumer, E117 is learned. Blockers: not differentiable (evaluation only), nuPlan devkit, no lane polygons, speed limit or agents. Use: re-implement the centre-line plus IDM baseline first (effort S), PDM-Closed-lite later.

Transformer planner over polygon tokens (20 centre points, on-route flag) with a state dropout encoder against the ego-motion shortcut; the paper has no map section, the input contract comes from the code. It is the published format our graph plus route probability can be cut into (adapters A1-A3), with a soft route embedding as convex mixture of the two flag embeddings. Blockers: no licence, nuPlan devkit, no connectivity input, roadblock-level flag, an estimated 8 times the weights of E117. Use: re-implement as a format test against E117.
extract: deep: code extraction later if needed

text: Reference lines from a route-restricted depth-first search over the lane graph serve as lateral queries; a contrastive loss uses causal negatives. The paper has no ablation of the reference lines, the route filter lives only in code. For us: scored path enumeration over the perceived directed graph with a soft route score, plus route-flip negatives; E117 is already near its oracle-route ceiling (0.34 vs 0.316 m), so gain is likely small. Blockers: DFS is a rule step, no licence; use at idea level (effort S): path features for E117.
extract: deep: code extraction later if needed

text: Lane-graph convolution: nodes are centre-line segments, four adjacencies (predecessor, successor, left, right) with dilated powers, 128 channels; on Argoverse minFDE 1.10 against 1.41 for plain graph convolution. Our directed edges map to predecessor and successor, left and right must be derived geometrically; E117 reads edge tokens by attention and no graph-convolution consumer was tried. Blockers: false forks and gaps corrupt the dilated adjacency powers, ground-truth-map evidence only. Watch: topology-aware consumer variant if E117 saturates.

Register-only entry (no note, note has little detail): the source table says MP3 predicts a dense probabilistic map (drivable area, lane-centre distance, lane direction) plus a route map and scores trajectories against it, closed-loop success 74.39 % against 22.56 % for a baseline. It is the precedent for dense output without discrete lane instances and for the route as a raster input, close to our dense head. Low relevance: other setting, text and table disagree on off-route rate. Context for the dense-plus-route interface, no action.

Vision planner: candidate trajectories from a bicycle model are scored by a hand-made safety cost, a learned cost volume and comfort terms, then GRU-refined; its BEV grid is 200 x 200 at 0.5 m on nuScenes, identical to our cached grid. It could serve as a dense-raster control for the graph consumer, which E117 does not test. Blockers: end-to-end camera training, sampling with argmin selection, L2 not comparable with our path error. Watch: raster control only if the consumer is challenged.

Two-stage end-to-end planner: MapFormer map queries (Hungarian matched) reach the plan only through MotionFormer, and the planner cross-attends BEV plus ego query and command; the planning table does not isolate the map module (L2 1.131 to 1.004 m for all intermediate tasks). Registered as interface reference K88 for the map-to-planner hand-over; our matched sparse decoder was dropped (E31 / E32). Blockers: Hungarian matching, 125 M parameters at 1.8 FPS, mmcv stack. Context for the interface choice, no action.

Vectorised planner: the ego query attends predicted agent and map vectors; training-only hinge constraints use the predicted points (boundary distance 1.0 m, lane direction within 2.0 m) and the gradient reaches the selected map points. The constraints cut L2 only from 0.76 to 0.72 m, and our planner loss through positions (E121) gave no gain, so the idea is already tried (K89 interface reference). Blockers: the boundary term needs road boundaries, Hungarian-matched map head, ego-status leakage on nuScenes. Context, no action.

Probabilistic planner: a vocabulary of 4096 trajectories is scored by planning tokens that attend vectorised map, agent and traffic tokens, with a navigation embedding and a conflict loss that pushes down entries leaving the road. The map reaches the planner only through tokens and those labels; there are no nuScenes planning numbers (CARLA Town05 Long DS 85.1). Blockers: needs a trajectory vocabulary, route enters as a command only. Context (K127 interface reference): the command-only contrast to our lane-level route attribute.

Register-only entry (no note, note has little detail): the source table says predicted map elements (centre-lines, dividers, boundaries, crossings) become scene-graph nodes of the planner, with nearest-neighbour agent-to-map edges (K=8) and the command joined to ego status; L2 / collision 0.68 / 0.12 against 1.22 / 0.47 for VAD in their reproduction. Closest published map-elements-as-nodes hand-over, but no lane-connectivity edges, graph ablation on motion prediction only, tables disagree. Context (K91 interface reference), no action.

Sparse end-to-end driving: map polylines (100 x 20 points) are instances like agents, and the ego instance attends agents and map in command-specific modes; L2 0.61 m, collision 0.08 % at 9 FPS with 85.9 M parameters. It confirms that stacks hand map instances to the planner by attention, which E117 already does with edges, route probability and ego motion (K90 reference). Blockers: Hungarian-matched instances, from-scratch trainable perception, mmdet3d stack. Context, no action; the matched sparse decoder was dropped in E31 / E32.

Prediction models read the mapping network's stored BEV feature grid instead of decoded vectors (HiVT with MapTR minADE 0.4234 to 0.3617, up to 73 % faster). This is our situation, a consumer on frozen cached BEV features: E117 reads edges, route and ego motion but no features sampled at the vertices. Blockers: staged training so the consumer does not shape the BEV, no GT-map comparison, PL49 warns about dense BEV input. Watch: sample the cached 39 channels at vertices as an E117 variant. TIER? closest to our frozen-feature setting.

Diffusion transformer over a lane tensor of 70 lanes x 20 points x 12 channels; the route lanes (25 x 20 points) condition every block through adaptive layer norm; Val14 non-reactive score 89.87. A global route embedding is an alternative to our per-edge route attribute, but then the planner cannot tell which lane is the route, and wrong routes are not tested. Blockers: no edges used, boundary and traffic-light channels absent, nuPlan-only training, 100 m range. Watch: adaLN route conditioning as a consumer ablation (K97 interface reference).

Goal-driven flow matching: a goal point from a vocabulary is scored by distance and a drivable-area test, then conditions the trajectory generator; a shadow trajectory made without the goal flags unreliable goals. Useful for us: the end of the route-assigned lane set as a goal candidate, and the shadow pass as a label-free monitor of whether the route changes the plan (oracle goal gap 90.3 to 92.1, like our oracle route 0.316 m). Blockers: camera plus lidar NAVSIM, hard goal argmax. Watch (K94): idea for the consumer, not built.

Per-point Laplace scales of the predicted map become uncertainty queries for agent and ego attention and drive a trajectory filter; it adds 1.9 % parameters and lowers drivable-area conflicts (VAD 1.39 to 0.80 %). Our vertex validity (keep probability) is the analogue of 1/b but has not been fed to a planner (E120 keep gate exists for perception only), and we have no per-vertex position scale. Blockers: threshold unspecified, hard selection, end-to-end VAD stack. Watch (K49): validity as log-bias or token input to the consumer.

Mapping memory cross-attends the ego-status embedding to form a plan query, fused with a BEV branch by an ego-status-dependent weight; the trajectory loss also reaches the mapping module. It is a cooperative-driving system (DAIR-V2X), and on validation collision rose against its baseline (0.34 to 0.94 %), so evidence is thin. The gradient into the map side is what E119 / E121 tried without gain; K95 registers its ego-state gate idea (E115, E117). Context, no action.

Register-only entry (no note, little detail): the source table says planners often ignore the route command (Hydra-MDP NAVI head 69.6, 30.4 % ignored); it adds a binary compliance metric, a counterfactual-command dataset and a head predicting the last waypoint on a route lane. It matches our counterfactual-route test (E117d: 30 m point moves to a side road in 64 % of 51 frames), and route labels can come from the lane graph. Blocker: the NAVSIM camera-lidar planner is not reusable. Use: copy the compliance metric for route-flip tests.

Polylines of vectors with attributes, a polyline subgraph (max-pool) and one global self-attention layer over all nodes; no lane topology, 72 K parameters and 0.041 GFLOPs per target. It is the simplest encoder and robust to missing edges because it uses none, similar to E117's edge tokens (start, middle, end). Blockers: forks and merges are invisible, no official code, Argoverse agent prediction. Context: explains the token choice, no action.

Level-k interactive prediction and planning: each agent decoder is conditioned on the other agents' futures of the previous level, with a route reference path and a differentiable Gauss-Newton refinement; nuPlan test overall 0.8288. A differentiable refinement could post-process E117's path, but the game part needs agent predictions we do not make, and the planner has no connectivity input. Blockers: agents, nuPlan devkit. Context, no action.

Planners given target points steer towards the nearest point (about 25 % of decoder attention on that token); TransFuser with target points reaches 39 DS / 84 RC against 32 / 56 with commands (CARLA). Direct risk for our consumer: E117 depends strongly on the route probability (0.90 to 0.40 m), so it may follow the flag instead of the geometry. Mitigations: route-attribute dropout, shift and rotation augmentation. Watch: add them to the route-corruption sweep; CARLA evidence only.

A trajectory vocabulary (4096 / 8192) is scored by heads that imitate the sub-scores of the rule-based PDM simulation; the map is used offline for the teacher scores only and the student needs no map heads (PDMS 83.0 base, 91.0 scaled). A PDM-lite scorer on our graph could be distilled or used as a route-compliance auxiliary head, but only after the PL02 scorer exists. Blockers: needs a rule simulation per vocabulary entry, camera-lidar NAVSIM input. Context, no action now.

A rough navigation route (5 m spacing, 11 points near the ego) is encoded by direction and heading rather than position, because the route may deviate by metres; a target module scores candidates on reconstructed lane centre-lines. On nuScenes val L2 0.61 m against 0.72 m for VAD, turning scenes 1.40 against 1.88 m; no noise test of the path. Our consumer reads route probability per edge, the lane-graph version of this. Blockers: no code, argmax target, VAD training stack. Watch: direction-only route encoding for shifted maps.

Lane queries as double-edge lanes with a per-point planning flag; the planned path is the midpoint of flagged points. The per-point on-the-plan flag resembles our per-vertex route probability (E102-E104), but there is no topology between lanes, the route command handling is not described, and results are CARLA only (Town05 Long DS 91.1) with camera plus lidar and no code. Context: confirms the per-vertex flag idea, no action.

Dense BEV squeezed into 16 tokens modulated by the command through a squeeze-and-excitation gate, no detection or map supervision; nuScenes L2 0.75 m, collision 0.15 %, better than UniAD and VAD. A map-free planner reaching such open-loop numbers shows that these metrics cannot judge graph quality; its navigation-guidance ablation shows no clear gain. Blockers: trainable camera encoder, command only. Context: supports a planner-aware metric (PL02 test bed), no action.

Task-parallel transformer: 900 agent queries, 100 map queries and an ego query interact in every block, 6 plan modes trained winner-take-all; nuScenes open loop L2 0.40 m without and 0.33 m with ego status (Large). The ego-status gap supports our caveat on ego-motion shortcuts (K108), but the map side needs Hungarian matching, latency is 211.7 ms and the gradient into map queries is only inferred. Context, no action.

Planning as motion prediction: ego and other vehicles share a two-stage decoder over SparseDrive agent and map instance features grouped into zone subgraphs; nuScenes L2 0.39 m against 0.61 for SparseDrive. Map nodes enter only as SparseDrive instances and the model needs agents we do not produce; the note was read only up to the cut and no code was found. Low relevance: end-to-end trainable perception with instance matching, nothing beyond PL10 for our graph. Not relevant.

CaRL and a flow-matching policy render the route as a lane-level mask in a BEV raster; CaRL finds the policy largely ignores lane markings and abuses the route mask for steering, and drawing the route only inside intersections cut crashes (longest6 DS 64). This is our route attribute in raster form with the same shortcut risk as C18; neither paper perturbs the route. Blockers: RL / CARLA setting, raster rather than graph. Context: supports route-corruption tests, no action.

Twenty K-means planning anchors guide perception: guiding points of each anchor are projected into BEV and image coordinates as reference points for cross-attention, then refined near to far; dense BEV segmentation only, NAVSIM PDMS 90.2. Sampling features along the planned path is the same principle as our verified rays and fans, applied to planning; there is no lane graph. Blockers: trainable LSS encoder, image branch needs camera projection. Context, no action.

RAP uses rendered lane polylines only to create training views; DriveZero trains a privileged teacher on a local vector map and two route goal points, then distils into a camera-only student with a command and no map head (PDMS 94.8). Map-free leaders show that planner scores can be high without any lane graph, so graph quality is invisible in such benchmarks; a teacher on the GT graph could distil or score a consumer. Blockers: RAP about 888 M parameters, DriveZero RL on 96 GPUs. Context, no action.

Pixel-wise Gaussian logits on the BEV segmentation give a safety score per trajectory (minimum drivable probability along the path) that re-weights and filters diffusion proposals; NAVSIM PDMS 87.7, camera only. Our cached map-layer logits already hold a drivable probability raster, and a graph validity could weight path safety, so it could feed a drivable-area term of a PDM-style scorer. Blockers: relies on segmentation not a graph, DiffusionDrive decoder, no code, text and table disagree. Watch: scorer term in the PL02 test bed.

Encodes the OSM route as a 64-d vector, runs a route-led and a perception-led trajectory branch, and a gate picks one (route branch in 66 % of tests); ADE 1.82 against 2.19 for image plus kinematics. Closest published thing to abstention (trust route or perception), supervised by the error difference of two planner passes, which costs little with our 93 k-parameter planner; no controlled corruption test. Blockers: route is a global point list not a lane attribute, hard branch choice blocks gradient. Watch: gate test for the abstention item.

Renders ego-centric lane topology and traffic elements as a sentence, encodes it with a frozen BERT (110 M) and concatenates the tokens to planner queries. With VAD on nuScenes, ground-truth topology and topology predicted by TopoMLP give identical results (0.62 m / 0.16 %), so open-loop planning cannot resolve graph quality, which is why we want a planner-aware test (PL02). Blockers: text encoder, OpenLane-V2 annotations, no code. Context: motivates the test bed, no action.

Agent motion predictor in which each lane centre-line becomes independent segment vectors with attributes and no lane-to-lane edges; Argoverse minADE 0.66 (HiVT-128). It is the usual consumer of online maps on nuScenes through the PL15 pipeline and could test our graph as an external consumer; paper not read, only dataset code. Blockers: PyTorch 1.8 / PyG 1.7 pins, agent histories we do not predict. Watch: external consumer only if a prediction test is wanted. TIER? no K id and a predictor, tier 3 fits.
